subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct two questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The first has to do with peace keeping in general, and in particular the proposal of the U.S.S.R. I would ask the minister whether the acceptance of the Soviet proposal in its present form would not have the effect of placing peace keeping operations under the security council of the United Nations rather than under the general assembly, thereby permitting the U.S.S.R. to exercise a veto and to control peace keeping operations.
My second question has to do with the situation of the peace keeping force in Cyprus. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the fact that in the United Kingdom within the last 24 hours there has been a reference to the number of Greek troops which allegedly infiltrated Cyprus
about ten days ago, the number which I mentioned at the time by way of a question as 4,000? Is there not now confirmation of that, and what has the minister to say in that regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the last question, I heard the report mentioned this morning, and there is no confirmation of those precise figures.
With regard to the first question, it is true that in the Soviet proposal for the establishment of a permanent peace keeping body under the United Nations, the Soviet union apparently intends that the security council shall have exclusive authority in the matter. It is only fair to say that under chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations there is such a provision. But since the charter of the United Nations came into being the general assembly has brought into existence the procedure, under the uniting for peace resolution, which gives a residual authority to the assembly when the security council, having exercised the veto or having failed to act, takes a course which is not acceptable to the general assembly. Canada continues to regard peace keeping as the primary responsibility of the security council but, as I said last night in the external affairs committee, Canada would feel that the general assembly, in the contingencies I have mentioned, should not be deprived of the right to act when the security council has failed to do so.

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: With the purport of what the minister has said I am in agreement, but he has not answered my question. Would not the acceptance of the Soviet proposal in its present form have the effect of obliterating that residual power which has developed whereby under certain circumstances the assembly can act?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. The veto is now embodied in the security council and is exercised by the great powers. The uniting for peace resolution was adopted after this power was given to the security council, and the general assembly acted notwithstanding. So my view, and it may be an arguable one, is that such would not be the situation.

Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Could I ask the secretary of state whether he has received from the Soviet union directly or indirectly the terms of their proposal, and could such terms be made available to us so we can study them? Also may we have some statement from the minister as to what is the reaction of the Canadian government to this proposal?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have not had a formal communication from the Soviet union. Other countries have not received their copies. It may be that the ambassador wishes to deliver it personally. However, we have had the full text before us and have made a preliminary study of the matter. As soon as this proposal is formally before us, I will be happy to see that the full text of the proposal is tabled in this house for the consideration of hon. members.

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: A supplementary question. I would hesitate to think that the information the minister has at hand is not as up to date as what we receive in news bulletins, but the confirmation I have heard is that the British prime minister said that 4,000 Greek nationals did land on Cyprus and were dispersed in small groups to homes in the mountains, and that these landings coincided with the arrival of General Grivas on the island. Has the minister been in direct contact either with the Greek or the Turkish government about this critical and serious situation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can tell my hon. friend that the British prime minister did not make any such statement, and I can assure my hon. friend, as I have already indicated, that we have been in touch not only with the ambassadors of the countries concerned in Ottawa but we are in continuous touch with the United Nations, with our NATO partners and with other sources. This is not the place to confirm or deny figures which are given in this way. There is under way a very important deliberation in Geneva under the direction of the mediator, who is meeting with certain parties. This could be a very important meeting, and because of it I do not propose to go any further at this moment.

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the figure I gave ten days ago was one which has been used very authoritatively in various places except in this House of Commons. After this meeting takes place in Geneva today will the

minister remove the mystery regarding this matter? Certainly all over the world this is the figure which is being used, and used by individuals who have some knowledge, as the hon. member said a few moments ago. It is difficult to understand why the secrecy, except that when we brought it up originally the minister said there was no foundation for the whole thing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think in a matter of this vital importance we should and, I am sure all of us agree, weigh very carefully the significance of what we say. I can only say to my right hon. friend that the government has sources of information, as have other countries; we have to assess these, and this we are doing. There is not much to be gained, in my judgment, by public discussion as to whether there are this number or that number. I have indicated that we have expressed our deep concern, as other countries have, with regard to the presence of troops from other countries that have an involvement.
The meeting that is under way now is a vital meeting. It will not be finished today by any means. This very important meeting is under the direction of the mediator. There are other parties present, among them parties who are guarantors of the treaty of 1961. I would sincerely hope that as a result of this meeting the situation will become clearer and I hope more satisfactory. In any event Canada takes the position which other members of the NATO alliance take. This situation is one that calls for both Greece and Turkey to exercise every moderating influence they can in order not to complicate an important and difficult assignment given by the security council to the mediator.

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext: There is one other matter. Certainly Canadians, with 1,100 men there, are most anxious to be assured that the Canadian government has made very clear to the Greek government and to the Turkish government the fact, regardless of NATO relationships or otherwise, that it is a very serious matter for Canadians if there be a basis in fact for such incursions in that country.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
subsubtopic: LANDING OF GREEK TROOPS IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has already been assured, and I reassure him, that when I saw both Prime Minister Papandreou in Washington and Prime Min-iter Inonu in New York a few days ago, I made this unmistakeably clear, as I did to their ambassadors here a few days ago, and as the secretary general has done. I would remind the house of the statement made by

General Gyani the day before yesterday when he made his report to the secretary general, and of the statement of the secretary general in the United Nations the day before yesterday when he directed a formal appeal to both Greece and Turkey with regard to infiltration asking them to respond in a manner that would enable him to make a report to the security council.

Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of his statement in the house supporting United States activities in southeast Asia, I wonder if the minister is now prepared to give equally vigorous support to the proposal of the United Nations secretary general, U Thant, for the convening of the 14 nation Geneva conference in an endeavour to resolve some of the difficulties in southeast Asia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. friend would not want to give the wrong impression. I did not make any statement that warranted the suggestion that Canada had given its imprimatur to the full position taken by a friendly power in Southeast Asia, and particularly in Viet Nam. I said Canada agreed with the United States that there was a violation by the Chinese communists of the provisions of the 1954 Geneva accord and the subsequent agreement of 1962.
With regard to the appeal made by the secretary general for reconvening the 14 power conference, I am not convinced that a reconvening of that conference could result in any arrangement other than that provided in the Geneva accord and in the conference of 1962. Canada has made this view known, particularly with regard to the Polish proposal for a six power conference in respect of the situation in Laos. However, at the same time we have indicated that, notwithstanding this view, if it were thought desirable that there should be such a gathering we would cooperate.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the violation to which the minister refers has to do with the 1954 Geneva agreement, would it not seem logical that the signatories to that agreement should be called together rather than resorting to unilateral action by
Inquiries of the Ministry the United States, which is not itself a signatory to the agreement; particularly in view of the statement made by Mr. Bundy, assistant secretary of state for eastern affairs, to a subcommittee of the United States house committee that the United States may now find it necessary to send troops into Viet Nam? May I ask the minister if it would not be preferable to have the 14 nation Geneva conference reconvened, since they are the people who are the signatories to the agreement which is being violated?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The presence of United States military forces in South Viet Nam is the result of an invitation under the authority of the government of that country. It is not in any way related to the fact that the United States is not a signatory to the Geneva accord. What I sought to point out was that the necessary machinery exists in the agreements themselves which set up the international control commission in the three countries-of which commission Canada is a member-to deal with this very situation. If all parties concerned lived up to those accords, there would not be the critical situation in Indochina that confronts the world today. That is the situation.
However, I want to make it clear that, if it seemed a desirable way of trying to mitigate the difficulty Canada would be willing to attend such a conference. But we believe that, if the nations concerned would live up to the obligations to which they are committed in accordance with the procedure outlined in the agreement, we could bring about some pacification in this situation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know a debate is not allowed at this time, but I want to say to the minister that I agree entirely with the viewpoint and stand being taken by the Canadian government. I suggest to him that he might outline those terms of the agreement which, carried into effect, would bring about a solution of the problem in southeast Asia. If he would do that I think it would clarify the situation very much.

To provide for and authorize the purchase out of United States dollars paid to Canada, pursuant to the treaty between Canada and the United States of America relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, together with any protocol or exchange of notes relating thereto, of such obligations of the government of the United States as may be approved by the governor in council, and the subsequent disposition of such obligations; the amount which may be expended for such purchase not to exceed $254,400,000 U.S. notwithstanding that this amount may exceed or fall short of the equivalent in Canadian dollars, estimated as of May, 1964, which is, $275,149,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I undertook when this item came up to make an explanation of the way in which this financing would be handled. This item arises out of the Columbia river treaty. The United States has agreed to pay on or about October 1, 1964, contemporaneously with the exchange of ratification of the treaty, $254.4 million U.S. in a lump sum as payment for the Canadian share of the downstream benefits of hydroelectric power. If the funds are paid over earlier, they are subject to a discount of 4| per cent per annum.
The Columbia storage power exchange, a non-profit organization of the power producers and users concerned, which is expected to raise the necessary United States funds, will pay to the government of Canada the United States funds as was agreed with the United States last January. The agreement is contained in the "attachment relating to terms of sale". As soon as the government of Canada receives the United States currency we will pay the Canadian dollar equivalent to the government of British Columbia, except that British Columbia may choose to receive some of the funds in United States currency in order to redeem some outstanding United States debts.
Accordingly- the government of Canada is seeking authority to pay out of cash on hand or from the proceeds of borrowings a maximum of $275,149,500 in Canadian funds to British Columbia, and will have a maximum offsetting asset of $254,400,000 in United States funds.
As I have said, British Columbia may prefer to receive some of the funds in United States currency in order to redeem United

States dollar obligations. To the extent that this takes place, the amount of Canadian funds to be made available by the Canadian government to British Columbia will be reduced. The amount of United States securities to be purchased will likewise be correspondingly reduced.
In my budget speech of March 16 last I mentioned an amount of $220 million Canadian as my estimate of our cash requirements in this fiscal year in connection with the Columbia river treaty lump sum payment. This was based on the assumption that British Columbia would require a payment of $50 million in the form of United States funds. The remainder of the lump sum payment, $204.4 million U.S., is equal to about $220 million in Canadian funds.
Except in one respect the arrangements will be similar to what happens whenever there is an increase in Canada's official holdings of foreign exchange reserves. Normally increases in Canada's official holdings of foreign exchange other than gold are invested by the exchange fund of the Minister of Finance in short term securities of the United States government. It is important to note that according to United States official statistics, increases in Canadian holdings of such short term securities would constitute part of the United States balance of payments deficit.
To avoid increasing the United States deficit in this way, Canada agreed with United States authorities last January that we would invest the proceeds of the lump sum payment in medium term non-marketable securities of the United States government. These securities, being non-marketable, will not be held in Canada's exchange fund account but will be held in a special account of the Minister of Finance. As the securities mature, it is expected that the proceeds will be taken into the exchange fund and invested in short term United States government securities in the normal way. The effect of this entire approach will be to even out the flow of funds into our reserves and to spread the impact of the transfer of so large a sum of money on the United States balance of payments over a longer period.
Arrangements in non-marketable securities have been made between the United States government and a number of other governments in recent years.
It should be pointed out that while the non-marketable securities mentioned above will not form a part of Canada's official hold-

ings of foreign exchange, they will constitute an important backstop for our reserves, and will add to our ability to marshal adequate resources in the event of a drain on our foreign exchange reserves. Although we do not anticipate any such drain, experience over the past few years has shown that our exchange position can become exposed to sudden and unexpected pressures from time to time.
The exact schedule of maturities and interest rates on these special securities remains to be worked out with United States authorities. Interest rates will be related to, but probably somewhat above, the market rates prevailing in the United States at the time of the issuance of the securities.
A question has been raised as to the cost to the government of Canada of acquiring these special United States securities. Such a cost would be regarded as being the difference between the interest paid by the Canadian government on the Canadian money raised to pay British Columbia and the interest received on the corresponding amount of United States dollar securities to be held by the government of Canada. Assuming that the lump sum payment is invested in medium term United States government securities, and assuming that the required amount of Canadian funds is obtained by the sale of Canadian securities of similar maturities, the difference between the interest rate earned in the United States and the interest rate paid in Canada would be in the neighbourhood of one half of one per cent on the basis of current yields. Assuming that the lump sum transfer was of the order of $220 million Canadian, the interest cost of the arrangement would be $1.1 million per annum.
However, two points need to be emphasized. First, costs of this nature are always incurred when the government increases its exchange reserves. In fact, because normally our exchange reserves are invested in market securities at slightly lower rates of interest than those contemplated for these special securities, the cost of this particular transaction is appreciably less than it would have been if our normal reserves had increased by an equivalent amount. Second, as I have already emphasized, these securities will form an important backstop to our exchange reserves. For quite different reasons in each of the past two years we have experienced heavy pressures on our exchange reserves. While we do not anticipate further speculative pressures, experience does sug-
Supply-Finance
gest the importance of being able to marshal adequate resources at all times.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in this phase of the minister's statement as to the purpose of this estimate. I must say that I am sure it comes as a surprise to some of us who realize that the government is in effect introducing legislation because this is an increased charge against the exchequer about which we were not told in the committee on external affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if I may clear up that point. The government, as my hon. friend knows, has authority to invest in Canadian securities. We also need, in this case, authority to invest in these medium term United States securities.

I fully understand that. This is, in effect, introducing legislation. You will remember that in the committee on external affairs the Secretary of State for External Affairs was most emphatic that this treaty was an executive act, that it was not necessary to come before parliament. I want to take this opportunity to say that a member of our party who is versed in these matters raised the question during his remarks in a debate in the house.
I should like to quote, Mr. Chairman, from page 67 of the minutes of evidence of the committee on external affairs for Tuesday, April 7, 1964:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I was simply going to ask the minister if when the former administration suggested that the treaty be put before a parliamentary committee, it was prepared to have it altered in any way?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course not. The treaty was signed in Washington by the President of the United States, by the secretary of state for the United States, by the Prime Minister of Canada, and by the Minister of Justice. The treaty was not in that form submitted to parliament because there was not an opportunity to do so. But under our practice, the government of the day takes its responsibility. It negotiates a treaty with another country and it takes its responsibility, and having taken its position and responsibility, then it asks parliament to approve or to reject. That is the constitutional position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Is it not correct that ratification is an executive act, or an act of the executive?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is right. There is no law which requires us to come to parliament or to refer the matter to a committee.
Some of the members of our group suggested that we were of the opinion, Mr. Chairman, there should have been a bill with the introduction of the treaty; it should not have been by means of a resolution which the house could simply endorse or reject. We claimed that this treaty was changing the law of the

Supply-Finance
land and was affecting the rights of certain Canadians. To support my argument in that connection I should like to read a few extracts. I think what is happening today proves we were correct. This is an estimate; this is legislation by estimate. The Minister of Finance admits that, does he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I said, this comes under the loans section of the supplementary estimates. All we are asking for is authority to invest these United States funds in short term and medium term United States securities. We have not got that authority to make investments in United States securities, and it is that for which we are asking.

Of course there will be a bill following these supplementary estimates.
Some well informed people looked up this question, and I should like to quote two or three authorities. The first article I should like to quote is by A. Lawrence Lowell, entitled "The Government of England", volume 1, page 22:
The crown...has power. ..to conclude treaties, save that, without the sanction of parliament, a treaty cannot impose a charge upon the people of change the law of the land, and it is doubtful how far without that sanction private rights can be sacrificed or territory ceded.
I am very interested to note that the hon. member for Kootenay East is paying attention to my remarks. I hope he stays until the vote comes on these estimates. There is a footnote to that citation which cites Anson, Law and Custom of the Constitution, volume 2, pages 297-99 and Dicey, Law of the Constitution, page 393. In my edition of Dicey the passage on the subject seems to be at page 460, where Dicey says that it is even open to question whether the treaty-making power of the executive might not in some cases override the law of the land. He gives a footnote reference to a judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council in 1892 which, however, refers only to treaties of peace and other treaties akin to them, as to which the judicial committee refrains from expressing an opinion.
Then I should like to quote Bora Laskin of the faculty of law, University of Toronto, who in his book "Canadian Constitutional Law", second edition, 1961, at page 270 quotes Chief Justice Duff:
But it is no part of the prerogative of the crown by treaty in time of peace to effect directly a change In the law governing the rights of private individuals, nor Is it any part of the prerogative of the crown to grant away, without the consent of parliament, the public moneys or to impose a tax or to alter the laws of trade and

navigation, and It is at least open to the gravest doubt whether the prerogative includes power to control the exercise by a colonial government or legislature of the right of apropriation over public property given by such a statute as the British North America Act.
That is what we are doing with respect to this treaty and with respect to the effect of this item. In addition, Mr. Chairman, I want to quote an extract from "The Law of Nations-Cases, Documents and Notes", published in 1938 and edited by Herbert W. Briggs of Cornell University. In chapter 10 of that textbook, entitled "The Law of Treaties", at page 433 under the subtitle "Treaties as Internal Law" Professor Briggs notes:
In another group of states, legislation is necessary before treaties affecting private rights become internal law which the courts will enforce. Thus Picciotto writes with reference to British practice that, whatever be the theories, there is an "undoubted modern practice of incorporating all treaties affecting private rights in acts of parliament".
This is the contention of the members of this group. The treaty should have been incorporated in an act of parliament as was done in the case of the boundary waters treaty of 1909, and as has been done in the past by the introduction of schedules to bills involving a number of treaties that have been ratified by the house. I wish to refer also to Picciotto, page 71, also Walker v. Baird (1892) A.C. 491, and to A. D. McNair who asks the question "When do . .. treaties involve legislation" and then goes on to explain the basis, which is very similar to the previous argument I have advanced.
I also wish to quote an extract from "Principles of British Constitutional Law" by Emden. Dealing with the external affairs function of the British executive Emden has this to say at page 15:
.-it is generally deemed advisable by the executive to obtain the sanction of the legislature to treaties, concluded in time of peace, which involve important cessions of territory-
Which this does in effect.
-the imposition of taxation-
Which these increased costs to the government will mean.
-a grant from public funds, the amendment of existing laws of trade or navigation, or interference with the private rights of the subject.
I have quoted from these few authorities in support of the contention of the members of this group that this treaty should have been introduced into the house as a bill, in which case the house would have had the opportunity to deal with the various clauses,

and the schedules should have included the agreement with the government of British Columbia just the same as agreements with other governments with respect to taxation have been included in schedules to bills.
I have a long way to go, today, Mr. Chairman, so I hope you will bear with me. Since the treaty was dealt with in the committee and since it was last dealt with in the house there have been certain changes in circumstances and certain things have happened about which members of the committee were not informed, and which in some instances I am sure the government had no idea were going to occur.
In this connection I want to quote from some correspondence that has taken place between General McNaughton and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think these letters should be placed on the record because they put the picture in true perspective from our point of view. I wish to quote a letter under date of June 3, 1964, addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to these letters in themselves being tabled, because they represent an interesting exchange that will have historical value if nothing else, but this matter has been decided by parliament. The treaty has been approved by a committee and by parliament, and any argument directed toward the treaty is completely out of order. My hon. friend is in order, of course, to discuss the matter which has been raised in the estimate by my colleague the Minister of Finance, but to go into the treaty now is contrary to the rules of the house. Parliament has taken a decision.
You are still taking a decision.

My hon. friend must address himself now to whether this particular item in the estimates should or should not be accepted.

Mr. Chairman, I definitely disagree with the opinion expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I fully expected him to make that argument, but I am giving reasons why we are opposed to this increased financial burden on the
Supply-Finance
people of Canada as the result of this item in the estimates. I am giving the reasons for requesting in the first instance that this matter be brought before the house in the form of a bill rather than a simple resolution with regard to which the house only had the opportunity to say yes or no, with no opportunity to amend as in the case of a bill, something to which we had looked forward. In that connection I believe I have the right under the rules of the house to place before the committee the reasons for my objection to this procedure and to this item.
I now proceed, Mr. Chairman, to read this letter addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Just hold on a minute. We have a letter here dated June 3, and surely this is after our discussions. I do not have to go back too many years to recall when the hon. gentleman was advocating the very opposite of what he is now saying.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I can shorten this. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And a protocol.

I submit that the resolution which was passed by the house does not put the treaty into effect unless this estimate is passed.

Without this estimate the treaty is only paper. Therefore, surely this committee has the right to go into any departure from the treaty or *any events which have transpired since passage of the resolution. It seems to me the hon. member is quite in order and ought not to be restricted to the narrow base suggested by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I may say a word on this. Under the treaty the Canadian government will receive 254 million United States dollars. All this estimate covers and all it asks for is authority to invest those dollars in medium term securities. That is all this estimate deals with.

The minister says that is all that is asked for. It is a good deal to ask for, and it seems to me that before the committee approves the authority which the minister is seeking we have a right and an obligation to look into the extent of the use to which this money will be put to see if it is in keeping with the treaty which was approved by resolution of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think I should remind hon. members of the second part of citation 148 (2) at page 126 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which, in part, says:
It is irregular to reflect upon, argue against, or in any manner call in question, in debate, the past acts or proceedings of the house-
I recognize that in discussing this item we would have to draw a fairly fine line between the actual proceedings which took place in the external affairs committee, the decision made in the house and the vote now before the committee, but I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West would not be in order if he were to call into question the decision taken by the house. However, if in discussing the item before the committee he wishes to make comments regarding the purpose for which this money is being allocated, that would be in order. But I would question his being in order if he were to rehash the whole debate on the resolution dealing with this particular point.
May I ask the Minister of Finance a question. What would happen if this supplementary estimate did not pass? What would happen with the cheque you were going to get from the U.S. government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The 254 million United States dollars received would be converted into Canadian dollars and deposited in Canada. Then the equivalent Canadian dollars, 275 million, if it were so desired and if the com-
Supply-Finance
mittee approved, would be used to buy U.S. dollars which could be put into the exchange fund or, as this item suggests, held separate in the form of medium term U.S. securities. The government has the authority to add to the exchange reserves but it has not got the authority to invest in medium term nonmarketable securities, and this is all that is being asked now. From the standpoint of our finances and from the standpoint of a backstop to our exchange reserves this is a highly desirable move, and I have no hesitation in asking authority to pursue it.

It is not absolutely necessary, as I understand it, for this supplementary estimate to pass in order to receive a cheque from the United States. What we are dealing with here is something subsequent to the transaction; it is an administrative problem which would exist after having received the money from the United States, not before. Am I right in that assumption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is my understanding.
Must the Canadian investment be in United States securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I understand it, the United States authorities are not anxious to see a sudden drop in their exchange reserves of $254 million at one time. They have a balance of payments problem, as we have, and we are doing our very best to meet each other's difficulties. We think it makes sense from their point of view, and we wish to accommodate them. If we do so, we hope they will accommodate us on occasions when we have a problem. It is one of the ways in which things should be worked out between two friendly neighbours.

Is it not a fact that we too have a problem with regard to the international balance of payments? The first quarter of this year was another $100 million behind last year. The minister in his explanation said we were not getting as many American tourists up here as Canadians were going abroad. He has put the case for the United States government. Why not put the case for the Canadian government; because if our balance of payments is getting behind, surely to goodness this money would be better brought into Canada, held here and invested in Canadian securities. That is the only point I have to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have to distinguish in this transaction between our current account deficit in our balance of payments and the

Supply-Finance
over-all position. When we look at our overall position we find that Canada's exchange reserves have held up remarkably well. 1 think last month they increased by some $20 million. So we do not need this $254 million in one fell swoop. It is quite satisfactory to us to invest this amount in these medium term non-marketable United States securities which we can take into account if we should need to. If it is done in this way it will not cause a sudden drop in United States statistics. It is all right for us this way. It helps us, but we are doing it in a way which will accommodate the United States.
Once an investment is made in the United States, is it made on a term basis so that we in Canada will be able at any time to draw on that investment and bring it back to Canada and reinvest it here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I discussed that point two or three months ago with the United States treasury people and it was agreed between us that in practice if we needed this backstop it would be available. I am perfectly confident, from the conversations I have had that we could translate these non-marketable securities into marketable securities with the full approval of the United States authorities. I do not want to ask them for a formal agreement to this effect because then, I think, from a statistical point of view it would have to be shown as a reduction in their reserves. They do not want this to happen, and we do not need these funds at the moment.

One further question. This government feels this is the best way to handle the situation? In other words we are not being forced into it by the United States in any way, shape or form? Our present government feels they want to do it this way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. I can give the hon. member the assurance of the government and my personal assurance that this is a good way of doing it.

It is, of course, these very large increases in available energy from storage which is the source of the inherent flexibility of sequence IXa in the early period when firm power is an objective in Canada.
Moreover, later on when the systems mature it is the large stored energy in sequence IXa which provides a means of carrying the heavy seasonal upswings of hydroelectric generation instead of by installing the additional large, and expensive to operate, thermal plants which would otherwise be required.

Surely, Mr. Martin, such a gain in power in its most valuable form, not to mention the other advantages of sequence IXa such as the maintenance of Canadian control over East Kootenay waters, is a worth-while objective and evidences the need for renegotiation being insisted upon by the responsible government, the government of Canada.
I do not propose to go through again the detailed comments which I have made to you in our correspondence and to the external affairs committee in my presentations on the proposed Columbia river treaty and protocol and sale agreement because these are all reproduced in the committee's minutes. I merely state at this time that I reaffirm the views I have stated to you.
Also that I have examined the comments made by your adviser Mr. G. M. McNabb and it is my view that he has failed to appreciate the true import of the various clauses of the treaty and protocol in question and the importance and equity of the various proposals I have made in correction.
For example in my presentation the importance, in regard to flood control, of an effective and continuing deterrent to abuse and the limitation of the objective at the Dalles: this so that, as the U.S. continue to move out into the flood plain of the lower river, the operation of Canadian storage shall not be increased as would be the case under the present wording.
Also, in regard to power, X draw attention to my proposal that the treaty should be revised to implement the principle agreed to in the I.J.C. that benefits from the co-operative use of Canadian storage should be equally divided and that all forms of benefit should be included.
In this connection also I have recommended that annex A, paragraph 7, et sequence, which sets up a criteria of operation on a basis of optimization of system benefits, which is contrary to I.J.C. principles, should be replaced by a criteria which will provide for a "best use value" of Canadian resources in head and flow in Canadian at site generation as is customary in interconnection agreements between utility systems.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate and understand your comments on my remarks. I apologize if I transgressed. I did not mean to reopen the debate on the Columbia river treaty. I was trying to point out what the effect would be if this estimate were passed by this house, if this government were not alert to the situation and to the objectives of United States interests and to the policies of the government of British Columbia. Really they are very closely intertwined. I was just using this estimate to point out the possibilities in the future, without going into the question of the Columbia river treaty. However, sir, I am quite sure that both of us are inclined to look at this from different points of view. Naturally, coming from Newfoundland, Mr. Chairman, you would be very objective about the matter. I admit that at times I am not completely objective.
I just want to conclude my remarks on this point before dealing with another aspect of this item. I am doing this because I want the government to be on the alert and realize what is happening. I continue to quote:
The unwillingness of the Canadian government to support this Alcoa project was followed by development of a similar project by the Aluminum Company of Canada in northern British Columbia in the wilderness area of Kitimat-
Now, the background of that story is not any too well known. What happened in this connection was that Dr. Keenleyside, who was then deputy minister of the department in question, without authority of the minister, Mr. Winters, gave the president of the Aluminum Company of America a licence with regard to the exploration and development of this Rampart project, and so on. When this was discovered I happened to know that Mr. Howe was most indignant. The president of the aluminum company was invited to come to Canada, and at a dinner was told by Mr. Winters that the licence was going to be cancelled. Shortly afterward Dr. Keenleyside packed his bags and got a job with the United Nations.
This is all part of the same scheme. Regardless of our opinion of the Columbia, the purpose of these developments has always

been to build a power line from California to the Yukon and have a tremendous flow of British Columbia and Canadian power into the United States instead of having it go into a Canadian national grid. I take this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, because this is what I am confident is proposed for the future. I speak as a Canadian, and I speak as one from British Columbia who wants to see this power used to produce jobs in Canada, in British Columbia and in the Kootenays.
X have one other aspect, Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention before I conclude. This has to do with the question of compensation to persons affected. I trust the members of all parties will stand up and do their part to see that these people get justice. The Secretary of State for External Affairs told us he was assured that the persons affected by flooding from these dams would receive proper relocation or compensation therefore.
I have been asked by a large number of people along the Arrow lakes to raise this question in the house. Dr. Keenleyside came into the district and intended to speak to one or two chambers of commerce. This was not good enough for them, and they demanded that he speak at public meetings. They organized public meetings and he spoke at Edgewood and at Nakusp to between 350 and 400 people. He was battered with a barrage of questions which were not answered to the satisfaction of the people concerned. They were told that the there would be no replacement or relocation, and that compensation would be on the basis of market value.
I have a newspaper report here. I could read at length from it, Mr. Chairman, to indicate how very upset these people are. I happen to know that one of the farmers' institutes of the district has written to the Prime Minister bringing this to his attention. I know they have written other members. I have had letters also from the Castlegar to Revelstoke area. I am using this estimate as a means of bringing this to the attention of the house. To indicate what happened at this meeting, I should like to quote the headline on the article. "No Replacement Compensation says B.C. Hydro's Keenleyside". The article reads in part:
Residents of the reservoir flood basin will not be compensated area for area. Dr. Hugh L. Keenleyside, co-chairman of B.C. hydro, told an enthusiastic audience of 300 in the Legion hall Tuesday.
People who expect to get full compensation or replacement value for their homes will definitely not get it he said.

I am bringing this to the attention of the house and I trust I have the support of other members. After the assurance given in the committee on external affairs, after the statements that have been made by the chairman of the B.C. hydro authority and the speeches he made to the Vancouver board of trade and the Kelowna board of trade, this was a great shock to these people. I indicate this by quoting again from the article:
Mr. Frank Lewis of East Arrow Park told Mr. Keenleyside that he had been promised by the co-chairman one year ago that he and other senior citizens would get help in relocation because they couldn't afford to move.
"Tonight you have reversed your promise."
Then spokesmen from other areas got up. Finally one man, a veteran who has just completed paying for his home and was told he would get the market value, was told by Dr. Keenleyside that he would do what he could to assist him to borrow money to build a new home. This man said:
If you are going to rebuild Celgar's dumps with new ones, then you should also replace the old houses with new ones.
He also said:
I would like to make my position clear, sir. You'd better send a big man.
These people are very concerned indeed. I believe there is a responsibility upon the federal government to use its influence with the government of British Columbia and the B.C. hydro authorities to see that these people receive justice, are relocated and do not suffer in any way. They do not want to make a profit and they do not wish relocation at an improper expense to the B.C. hydro authority, but they want to be compensated so they will not suffer any actual loss because of this development. We are told this is a work for the advantage of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, you will recall that the member for Kootenay West was just making a plea for the concern of members of this house from all parts of the country for the situation he has been describing. I feel that the vote we have before us places some rather stringent limitations on the total amount that may be authorized to be spent, and does give us cause for concern about this situation that has arisen subsequent to the ratification of the Columbia river treaty by this house.

Supply-Finance
Some members who are present will recall the period when the St. Lawrence seaway was under construction and the reports that were made in the house with regard to how the people of the area affected by that development were being relocated, steps which in many cases involved the moving and relocating of people almost in complete towns. As a member from British Columbia at that time I enthusiastically supported the taking of equitable action with regard to the people who were involved in that development in the central part of Canada.
Now that the parliament of Canada has seen fit to authorize a type of development in British Columbia which involves the flooding out of many of the people in the Arrow lakes area, I feel that parliament certainly should be concerned to see that those people in that province are treated with equity equal to that which was extended and supported by parliament in the case of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I think the hon. member for Kootenay West has given us cause for a good deal of concern about some of the developments that have taken place since we saw fit to ratify the treaty. He has given us some cause to consider whether, if our fellow citizens in the area most immediately affected are to be treated with justice and equity, the liability on the part of the government which parliament is being asked to ratify will be adequately or properly discharged with the kind of limitation of figures found in the vote before us. In this situation I feel that one of the matters which should be of concern to us before we decide to pass this item is whether it will satisfy adequately the financial responsibility which parliament has a moral obligation to assume in connection with the development in the Columbia river valley which we earlier authorized to take place.

Mr. Chairman, I only want to say a few words on this item. I note in the estimate that we are being asked to transfer some of the money paid by the United States to the government of Canada. We are actually being asked to convert this money into U.S. dollars and to leave the amount in the United States. If you read the item you will see that it goes on to say:
...relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, together with any protocol or exchange of notes relating thereto, of such obligations of the government of the United States as may be approved by the governor in council...
We are now being asked to allow this money to remain in the United States, and I am won-

dering for what reason we were originally to be paid $254 million. If it was to assist in the development of the Columbia river project, then obviously we should not be turning this money over to that country even in the form of investment in short term bond issues of that country, but should be retaining it in Canada.
I think we are all concerned about the method used in dealing with the Columbia river treaty in the first place. A bill should have been introduced and the problem should have been completely understood. That matter has been decided, but in some respects it would appear that perhaps it has not really been decided after all. If we have this obligation for which we are paying $254 million in U.S. dollars, it would appear to me that we will be asked in a further estimate to provide that amount of money in Canadian dollars, which will make it that much easier for the United States to meet its obligations and create hardship to the same extent for the Canadian people.
Certainly the government of Canada was not to have this money in payment of its contribution in a national sense. Obviously the decision reached between the federal government and the United States government was that the development of the potential of the Columbia was a matter of provincial jurisdiction in Canada, and therefore the province of British Columbia had the right to make a call on the moneys paid.
In my opinion this will involve a further expenditure. In addition to the supplementary estimate we have before us now, it will very likely result in an additional estimate of an equal or greater amount. The amount of money we are generously lending the United States on a short term basis will have to be raised by the Canadian people in order to proceed with the Columbia river complex and we will be asked to vote a further amount. I believe the Canadian people will be very concerned about what is involved in this supplementary estimate. Neither the purpose nor the reason for this vote has been made clear to the public.
I think the matters raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West must be given very close scrutiny, and there must be a statement by the government that they intend to correct some of the faults already evident and which can be corrected by the sum of money being paid by the United States. This money was supposed to represent compensation paid to Canada for benefits that the Canadian people were losing.

Yet we are told that people in British Columbia, who are affected by the treaty and by the estimate we are discussing, are not being given reasonable or adequate treatment in the expropriation of their properties.
It would seem to me that the situation in British Columbia will involve problems similar to those that developed and were faced in other parts of Canada, particularly in relation to the expropriations made necessary by the flooding for the St. Lawrence seaway. In the general interests of a community expropriation can be used, but a bending over backward must take place in relation to the rights of individuals who suffer as a result of expropriation. In my view this amount of money was to be paid by the government of the United States to see that people displaced were treated properly.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

It appears to me there is some relationship between this supplementary estimate and the moneys which can be paid, and without having seen the exchange of letters we must conclude that there was a request from the United States government to the Canadian government to invest in these medium term securities. I am quite sure the United States government is as familiar with the situation in Canada as we ourselves, and knows our balance of exchange is no better than that of other countries and is becoming increasingly difficult as time goes by. The advent of a large sum like $275 million would be advantageous to our balance of payments, and the fact that it is not being used in this way is an indication that the United States has asked that the money be not removed from the American market.
It is unfair for the supplementary estimate to contain statements referring to the protocol

I believe we should use this money to provide adequate, and even better than adequate expropriations for those who are going to be affected by the terms of the treaty, and that we should keep the money in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should let some of the remarks that have been made in connection with this witch hunting pass unnoticed. Mr. Keenleyside, as a member of the hydro commission, has an obligation to the corporation and to the people. He is certainly not going to play Santa Claus, and that is to be expected, but we do have the commitment of members of the government that fair treatment will be given these people. This was mentioned in the external affairs committee and is a matter of record.
I asked the hon. member for Kootenay West whether these expropriations were subject to a board of referees. This is a practice that has existed over the centuries and when the time comes these people in the affected areas will not be asking for arbitration because they are going to get a better deal without going to arbitration. In so far as the statement of the hon. member for Kootenay West is concerned I want to make that correction. This is what I call witch hunting. We have had a long discourse on the evil thoughts of the Americans in connection with this whole matter, and there has been a suggestion of underlying currents.
What is wrong with having a power line from northern British Columbia and the Yukon, shall we say, to California? It is very nice down there, and maybe some people would like to go down there, live on their pension cheques and use some of the Canadian power. Again I mention that I would not like this passed without calling attention to the witch hunting that is going on in this committee.

Just before it passes I want to deal briefly with a matter that comes under the responsibility of the federal government. I may say we must acknowledge the fact that there are two members of the Social Credit party in the chamber and eight members of the Liberal party, so we are doing pretty well indeed.
Dealing with the question of relocation and compensation, the federal government has some responsibility with respect to the veterans affected. There will be 50 or 60 veterans affected by the building of the high Arrow dam. Some of them purchased properties under the Veterans Land Act and some purchased properties directly themselves, but as a result of Dr. Keenleyside's visit to the district they are very concerned. They held a meeting in the village of Nakusp attended by some 150 delegates, and I would like to read briefly from the Arrow Lakes News of June 25 with respect to the resolution adopted at that meeting. The article in question is headed, "Legion Convention gives Backing to Hot Replacement Question," and it reads:
The West Kootenay zone of the Royal Canadian Legion resolved to ask the Department of Veterans Affairs to provide professional assistance to those veterans which will be affected by the Columbia river development projects.
The resolution was presented by Branch 20, Nakusp, who were the hosts for the week end convention...
A general meeting of the Branch 20 membership voted unanimously in favour of the resolution:
Whereas the veterans residing in the flood basins of the Columbia river, who are to be affected by the treaty, will be at a disadvantage negotiating with trained officials of the B.C. hydro authority;
Whereas experience has shown great variance in allowances for similar properties received from hydro authorities for similar areas for no apparent reason;
Whereas these affected veterans are in fact negotiating for the interests of Veterans Land Act, National Housing Act. soldiers settlement board and others as well as those of their own;
Therefore be it resolved that the Department of Veterans Affairs be asked to provide professional

assistance to veterans affected by the Columbia river development projects.
Another resolution was adopted by the convention in the following terms:
With regard to displacement of persons living in the area to be flooded by the Columbia development projects:
Whereas it has been stated in verbal and written form by Dr. Keenleyside that market value will be the criterion used in the purchase of property of affected persons, and
Whereas the use of market value can mean a very great hardship on people who cannot afford to pay the difference between market value and actual cost of replacement; and
Whereas many veterans will be affected by the system of market value settlement;
Therefore be it resolved that the Royal Canadian Legion support the principle as follows:
When a person, or persons, are forced with the necessity of having to move; where a cash settlement is not suitable, that B.C. hydro resettle that person in accommodation not less favourable to that person at no cost to the person being resettled.
I bring those two resolutions to the attention of the committee because they were adopted at a zone convention concerned with the welfare of the veterans and of all those persons affected. The president of the Royal Canadian Legion of the province of British Columbia wired me in this respect as did the secretary of the branch concerned. I do urge that the government and the Department of Veterans Affairs particularly should bring their good offices to bear so as to assist these veterans in connection with expropriation or purchase. We recall what has been done in this regard by the national capital commission, which has in my opinion treated people very fairly and properly. We remember what was done in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. Every person who had to be relocated was relocated at no cost to himself. Houses were moved back, and in most cases new basements were built to the satisfaction of those concerned. Then, in connection with the Saskatchewan dam, those farmers and others who were affected were compensated not on the basis of market value but on the basis of the potential value of the properties they were being asked to leave on account of the development.
I do urge that the government through the Department of Veterans Affairs take whatever action it can to assist these veterans in the area to obtain justice, and I urge that the government as a whole should take an interest in the developments which are occurring in British Columbia with respect to these projects. I am sure that many interesting things are going to happen in the future. As I have said before, regardless of our opinions

respecting this treaty, no Canadian should be treated unfairly and unjustly to the advantage of the community as a whole. That is all I intend to say at this time and I thank the committee for listening to what I had to say, though I am sure they were at times somewhat bored with my repetition of these important matters.

In one serious respect I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West has given the committee a mistaken impression. We were told in the committee on external affairs when the treaty was before it that preliminary plans were in existence for all three Columbia dams and that working drawings existed with respect to two of them. We were also told that an engineering board would be reviewing and examining the plans and actual construction. I submit this five man board which has been appointed is in line with what we were told in the committee.

The hon. gentleman is confusing the permanent engineering board, which will represent Canada and British Columbia, with that other body. We were told nothing whatever about this new review commission. The hon. member is confusing this new commission or review board, which is the creature of the British Columbia hydro and power authority, with the permanent engineering board which will be responsible to governments for the whole project.
The hon. member for Spadina is right. We were told in the committee that this was to be set up. It is a special board to make sure that the work will be coordinated.

Would the hon. member for Spadina tell us, as a result of his knowledge of what is going on in the external affairs committee, whether that committee was given any indication of the announcement by the premier of British Columbia that he is now tying in a third river development requiring the damming of the Fraser river for hydro purposes? This is a most important matter. Now it appears we have moved away from a two river development to a three river development in British Columbia, and if my recollection of the plan put forward by General McNaughton is correct, it looks as though the premier is in part reverting to General McNaughton's plan. Can the hon. member tell us whether this is before the committee in any way or whether any representations have been made to the committee regarding this

new three river development, which was announced I think about four days ago by Premier Bennett?
Of course I can give no answer to that question. Furthermore, the question is completely irrelevant to the subject now being considered.

I can answer that question quite simply. It was given in the committee by Ray Williston in connection with the Fraser river engineering board report. Drilling and everything else has gone on on the upper Fraser. The testing is already being done.

I should like to return for a moment to the question of the financial obligations of the government of Canada and to the responsibility of this parliament generally in connection with the voting of money.
The particular point I wish to raise has reference to some of the observations made a little earlier in our proceedings by the hon. member for Cariboo when he referred to "time honoured expropriation proceedings". I am quite sure that the persons who will be responsible for the valuation of properties as a result of the development which is to take place will probably do a competent job. But the point I was trying to make earlier is that it depends upon the terms of reference which these people are given. I happen to have some recent experience with an incident involving the appraisement of land, and without entering upon a discussion of this matter I would refer to the situation arising out of the tidal wave disaster on the west coast. Appraisements there have been carried out on the basis of the depreciated values.
As I tried to say earlier, I think this committee should unanimously support the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay West that the people affected in the Arrow lakes area should be compensated on the basis of the cost of re-establishment and the replacement value of their properties. Certainly this is my understanding of the basis upon which compensation was available to people displaced by the St. Lawrence seaway project, and I was in this house at the time.
Since parliament has taken action by ratifying this treaty, and since it has assumed financial obligations in connection with it, as mentioned in the item before us, I suggest

Supply-Finance
this question of compensation is one of legitimate concern to every member of this house. We should be completely satisfied that those immediately charged with making compensation decisions have satisfactory terms of reference, and that those affected by their decisions shall be re-established as far as humanly possible without incurring any loss. The hon. member for Kootenay West has placed evidence on record to show that up to the present time this is not the policy being followed by the authorities charged with this responsibility within the province of British Columbia.
I suggest that this matter should be made abundantly clear. While we may be prepared to pass this item in the supplementary estimates at this time, it should be made clear at this time and there should be an indication in this house that unless certain changes are made in the policies which apparently have been followed up till now, this matter is by no means finished with as far as this parliament is concerned.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, surely I, as one of the members of the external affairs committee that sat and heard evidence in respect of this matter, would be prepared to vote against this estimate if I were not convinced that the B.C. government and the chairman of B.C. hydro were prepared to carry out the commitments they have made.
The hon. member for Kootenay West read from a newspaper report taken, I believe, from the Arrow lakes News, concerning a large meeting before which the chairman of the B.C. hydro appeared. The hon. member did not read all that was said at this meeting. The report of the meeting indicates that it is the intention of B.C. hydro to carry out its commitments.
I am not aware exactly what "area by area payment" means, but I would like to quote something that was said by Dr. Keenleyside in this regard. It is also related to what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said:
Dr. Keenleyside read from the water comptroller's terms for appraisals.. .fair market value of the property but will contain details of any circumstances which could be considered to give the property a value to its owner that is in excess of the fair market value.
"The appraisal report will also give details of circumstances that would entitle an owner to compensation for disturbance and moving expenses".
This means that many intangibles would be considered in each case. Sentimental attachment, back-breaking labour, home improvements, age,

employment, desire to move and many, many more will all have to be considered, he said.
This is substantially what was said in the committee. While no doubt there is some misunderstanding, and understandable misunderstanding, on the part of the people who are going to be displaced, I think the situation is clear. I think it is to the credit of these people that they continue to bring these matters before B.C. hydro and the province of British Columbia in order that there will be no relenting in their desire to fully compensate people for removals and any other losses that are anticipated. But to say that B.C. hydro and the B.C. government are going back on their commitments is completely without any foundation whatsoever.

Mr. Chairman, I represent those people and I am not going to sit here and have the member for Kootenay East suggest that I am not telling the truth. These people have written to me, hundreds of them; they are completely dissatisfied about what was said at the meeting that was addressed by Dr. Keenleyside. They got up at that meeting and said what I have quoted some of them as saying, namely that he had gone back on his word. They are very disturbed and put out about this matter. Also, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Kootenay East does not know it, the farmers of the district have sent a letter to the Prime Minister bringing these facts to his attention. You must remember that when you come to deal with a weekly newspaper nowadays, all weekly newspapers take a very neutral approach to public affairs-we have lost the old fire and brimstone we had 50 years ago- because they are all dependant on governments for advertising and things of that sort.
I speak with knowledge and conviction, Mr. Chairman. These people are most dissatified; and so far as the veterans are concerned, they expect the Department of Veterans Affairs to do what they can to assist them to obtain justice. As far as the rest of the residents are concerned, they hope that the government of Canada will do what it can to make certain that these promises which have been made will be kept. As I have said before, I am very interested in listening to the hon. member for Kootenay East as being an apologist for the government of British Columbia.
