DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Production and marketing-
15. Administration, operation and maintenance including the administration of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and contributions to agricultural organizations to assist in the marketing of agricultural products subject to the approval of treasury board, $2,190,400.

Mr. Chairman, when item I was passed I asked whether the Minister of Agriculture would let us discuss the subject of crop insurance under this heading, owing to the fact that there is no item in the main estimates specifically relating to crop insurance. One of the members who

wanted to speak on this matter is not present today so I am going to make a few remarks on that subject. My remarks will be brief and, I think, not controversial.
In 1959 we passed the crop insurance legislation to enable provinces to pass enabling legislation to set up crop insurance programs suitable to their conditions. As I understand it, there are at the present time four provinces with agreements on crop insurance, but others are interested.

Mr. Chairman, might I raise a point here. I understand, the problem of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is that the subject matter he wishes to discuss does not relate to one of the items in the main estimates. If I am correct in that, would it not be more appropriate to discuss the matter on item la of the supplementary estimates, which deals with departmental administration?

It would be satisfactory, I think, except that we are trying to get item 1 through the house. This is one of the matters which would have held us up for a considerable time but the minister agreed to let me discuss this on item 15. Unless this is another change of government policy I would just as soon discuss it now.
We have no objection.

This will only take a few minutes. Some of the provinces have taken advantage of this legislation, but it was apparent within a year or so after the legislation was passed that in those provinces where there is a one crop economy, such as the wheat growing areas, the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan were a little unhappy about putting in crop insurance to cover the whole province. The reason for this is clear. If the whole province were covered, in case of a major crop disaster the credit of the province would be extended under the conditions of the original act if the amount of money required to pay losses during any particular year exceeded the amount in the reserve fund of the crop insurance plan, then the province could come to the federal government and borrow the amount necessary to meet the shortages. The provinces felt that the requirements of borrowing from the federal government would reduce their power of borrowing, so felt reluctant to put the scheme in for the whole of the province.
Toward the end of the term of the last administration, this matter was before the

government. The proposal was that the provinces would reinsure for this amount with the federal government. The provinces would pay the federal government an amount of money on an actuarial basis as a premium to cover the costs of the reinsurance. This principle was under discussion and consideration at the time the government changed. I understand the minister intends to introduce a crop reinsurance bill. Without revealing any of the details of this legislation which may be intended to carry out this reinsurance on an actuarial basis, I wonder if he could confirm that this is the intention? If so, we on this side of the house will be satisfied, and I will say nothing more about crop insurances.
Yes, on June 8 we put this on the order paper, and I think it is very well covered in the suggestions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.

I should like now to go on to another subject, and on this too I shall be fairly brief. Vote 15 relates to the administrative costs of the agricultural stabilization board. I may have to come back to some individual questions, but I want to raise one major point in a general way in the hope the minister will give us some sort of lead on his thinking in this regard.
I am referring to the fact that in Canada today, generally speaking, agriculture is doing fairly well. The large area of weakness in the agriculture economy is concentrated in the low income areas. This is a major problem that will require the efforts of many people for many years to come. This is one problem. The other problem that is more immediate and has been here for the last eight or nine years is the difficulty of the dairy industry. The situation in the dairy industry cannot be described quickly, but suffice it to say that in the main we have an industry across Canada that is not in a serious situation, if you look at the over-all statistics. The surplus production from the industry is roughly 6 per cent to 7 per cent. However as a result of the fact that this surplus bears on those members of the dairy industry who have not got a fluid milk contract, the situation is desperate for them.
The previous government tried to cope with this situation by taking action under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. However we recognized as we were coping with that situation that adjustments would have to come as experience dictated. Without going into all the ramifications of the support price 20220-338$
Supply-Agriculture
policy of the agricultural prices board in connection with the dairy industry, I should like to focus my remarks on the pressure points of butter. It is recognized I think that the problem of the purely butter producer is almost hopeless. The consumer will not pay the price based on the 64 cents support price, therefore the consumption of creamery butter has fallen off. It was obvious that the price to the consumer had to be brought down to get him back into the habit of buying butter. This we did by a policy of keeping the support price to the farmer at 64 cents a pound and by letting the consumer have butter at the wholesale level of 52 cents a pound. This was, in effect, a consumer subsidy of 12 cents a pound to encourage the consumer to buy more butter.
The figures we have indicate that this policy was a success. I should like to make two points clear. First of all, a person who is in the business of producing butter, by itself, cannot make money at 64 cents a pound. Since the consumer who buys the product will not pay that price this means that we are up against what seems to be an insoluble problem. In the days when I was minister the department looked at many solutions to this problem and selected two or three that seemed promising. Every one of those solutions that seemed promising seemed to me to be based on the premise that there had to be something done by the farmers themselves to make the work of the senior governments effective.
In the case of milk, the provincial governments, under a provincial statute, guarantee a fair price to the producer of milk who is putting his milk into the fluid milk market. Using very round figures, the price for milk in this market is from $5 to $5.50 per 100. The price goes higher in some cases and a little lower in others. This I think the farmers would agree is essentially a fair price. However the farmer who is not lucky enough to have a milk contract receives an average price that fluctuates between $2.50 per 100 and $3 per 100 if he is in the business of shipping manufactured milk such as to a cheese factory. I am not attempting to be precise when I use these figures; it is just to give you the picture.
We know from the most casual observation that no matter how efficient a farmer is, even if he had 25 good cows and was running a very efficient establishment, at a price of $3 per 100 pounds, or less a farmer cannot make a living. This is an essential economic fact he faces. In order to try to bring about an adjustment we have used the Agricultural

Supply-Agriculture
Stabilization Act and tried to direct production into those forms for which there is a better market and which would give higher returns to the producer. I think, in all fairness, the Agricultural Stabilization Act has achieved a great deal. It has pioneered a whole series of new agricultural techniques to try to raise the income of farmers without costing the treasury an inordinate sum of money.
This does not mean that we have to say that the agricultural stabilization board has finished experimenting. I would suggest in this connection, that is in connection with the dairy industry, that the stabilization act could be used even better. We inaugurated a program of paying consumer subsidies on butter, for example. At that time I made it very clear to the provincial governments and to the dairy producers that this effort by the federal treasury to help sell more butter at great cost would be done as long as the farmers were making efforts themselves to get together and form some sort of national organization to help themselves. Now, for obvious reasons, this program of farmers to help themselves was centred in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario where the dairy problem is one of the prime interests of the people in the agriculture industry. The province of Quebec undertook to introduce legislation to enable the farmers to form a single organization in that province. The province of Ontario, through its minister of agriculture, organized a series of meetings with the four main dairy organizations in that province in an effort to try to bring about a single dairy organization that could co-operate with the Quebec organization and bring about relative harmony in marketing so far as the two adjoining provinces are concerned.
The next step was that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture called a dairy conference under the chairmanship of the late Dr. Hannam which was held in the city of Ottawa in the spring of 1963. This conference decided to move toward a national dairy policy. It was recommended that a committee of 16 be set up to help to draft a national dairy policy, with five members of the committee from the national dairy council, five representing the dairy producers, five representing the provincial governments-they having divided the country into areas-and one representing the federal government. To my knowledge that committee has either never met or certainly has made no progress report to the public.
In this period of adjustment we are trying to help the dairy farmers by subsidizing the

price of butter to the extent of over $40 million a year. This subsidy was given with the idea that at the provincial level and the farm level there would be a continuing effort to try to solve the problem by establishing a national dairy policy, which could take several forms.
I have almost completed my remarks, Mr. Chairman, but when we are discussing the administration of the stabilization board I believe we should hear what the policy of the government is in relation to the over-all dairy situation. We want to know if there is any activity at the provincial and farm levels to meet conditions that were well understood when we advanced the heavy subsidy on butter. I am not making these remarks for the purpose of causing any trouble between the provinces and the farm organizations. I make them because I know that unless we do have some rational dairy policy in Canada the great majority of the farmers in the dairy business, the 55 per cent in Ontario for instance with less than 13 cows, and the even greater percentage in Quebec with less than 13 cows, cannot be asked to continue indefinitely waiting for some action.
It is true that the difficulties are great. It is true that the heaviest responsibility falls on the provincial ministers to give leadership in their provinces in creating single dairy organizations in each province, so that a national organization can be formed with some opportunity to work out policies that will provide some control over the production and marketing of the products of the dairy farms. I suggest that the problems of low income farmers, mostly in eastern Canada, and the problems of the dairy industry are very closely related and that the test of any minister of agriculture of Canada will be how well he provides leadership in getting the provinces to continue their movement toward a single dairy organization within each province, which organizations can then sit down together and see if they cannot work out a national dairy policy within the next two or three years. I should like to know what the minister's thoughts are with regard to a national dairy policy and how he intends to use the agricultural prices stabilization board as part of the machinery to help to solve this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I assure the hon. member that we do recognize the problems he has mentioned. This committee has met four times, the last time in June, and the

next meeting will be in seven or eight weeks time. Its members are actively engaged in trying to formulate some policy that will protect producers in so far as prices are concerned. As the hon. member recognizes, the big problem of course is price, and there has been some improvement in this field. But I should like to assure the hon. member that the committee which represents all levels, the producers, the provinces, farm groups and the federal government, which has a representative, has met four times since the 1963 meeting. Its last meeting was in June and it will be meeting again at the end of September or the beginning of October.

I have one or two more precise questions. Has the federal government put forward any inducements to encourage the members of the committee to move faster in working out a national dairy policy? In referring to inducements I am not overlooking the fact that we put forward a $40 million inducement for them to get together, but I think they should be reminded that this inducement is conditional upon their moving forward. I should like to know from the minister what policy he has that will make the farmers of Ontario, with four separate organizations, want to get together to form a single organization and work in co-operation with the province of Quebec.

I can assure the hon. member that we do have this in mind and that we are moving forward in this direction. There are many problems. There are many people who, from a regional point of view, do not agree with what might be a good over-all policy. These are big problems, as the hon. member knows, but we are working toward what we think will be a much happier position in so far as the dairy farmers are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of the fact that we are now considering item 15A to discuss briefly a particular point which, in my opinion, affects the agricultural economy in the Saguenay district. Naturally, like many other areas, that area is faced with marketing problems.
In that district, most farmers are engaged in dairying and their products obviously include butter, cheese and a very small quantity of powdered milk.
Farmers have never been quite able to understand the government's attitude concerning the marketing of such products. In
Supply-Agriculture
fact, if there is a surplus of butter, one year, in Canada, the year after we are faced with an overproduction of cheese. As a result, the government pays subsidies on butter one year and on cheese the following year, so that our farmers can never know from year to year which of the two products they manufacture will be subsidized. Because of those surpluses, either of butter or of cheese, our farmers are confused, unable to decide whether they should produce butter or cheese or whether they should give up dairying altogether.
Mr. Chairman, item 15 reads as follows:
Marketing of farm products.
I also note that an amount of $35,000 was appropriated for this item last year and it seems that this year, no need was felt to resort to marketing-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, are we dealing now with vote 15?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
We have finished all the other votes up to that point?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I wish to draw the attention of the hon. members to the fact that the house is now considering vote No. 15 -production and marketing administration.

Mr. Chairman, that is precisely the subject matter with which I would like to deal. I see that, last year, an amount of $35,000 had been allocated under that item-marketing-while this year the amount allocated is only $20,000.
I am particularly interested in this matter, because, after all, the main problem facing our farmers today is precisely the problem of getting a stabilized market, a steady market for their produce.
Mr. Chairman, I think the Department of Agriculture should consider as most important the matter of finding markets for farm produce.
At the present time, the farming industry in the Saguenay area includes dairy farming and potato growing; and very soon now, the farmers of that area will be able to put on the market their production of blueberries.
I was reading recently a report published by Hon. Mr. Courcy, the Quebec minister of agriculture, to the effect that he would have to postpone his project to establish blueberry patches in the Saguenay peninsula, under ABDA, because of the uncertainty of

Supply-Agriculture
markets. Now, I am wondering to what extent this federal government is interested in this problem which the Quebec farmer has to face, and more particularly, the farmer in the Saguenay area, who is asking himself if he should give up dairy farming. When there are surpluses of milk, cheese and butter, the farmers are told: You should take up some other type of farming, you should produce something else, you should diversify your production.
Mr. Chairman, the farmer is quite prepared to diversify his production, to do something else, but he should, at least, be given the assurance that he will be able to sell on Canadian or foreign markets what he is requested to produce, and sell it at a reasonable price which will make it possible for him to live a decent life.
In my opinion, by having such a small amount earmarked for marketing research, the Department of Agriculture is simply missing an opportunity to use one of the means at its disposal to assist eastern agriculture, that of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. This question of markets is closely related to the present problem.
I was listening a while ago to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), the former minister of agriculture. Indeed, I always enjoy listening to him, because he speaks like a level-headed person and seems to be especially aware of farm problems. I like the suggestions he makes and when, a while ago, he said we should endeavour to unify our farm organizations in Quebec as they did in Ontario, in order to succeed in establishing a stable farm policy, I found myself in complete agreement with him on that point. I believe this is the way to a rational policy which would be acceptable to all the people concerned. However, until that feat is accomplished-because it will certainly be one to achieve that unification- we cannot let things deteriorate further.
The Department of Agriculture certainly has, on the federal level, a great responsibility, as stated so well this morning by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who is responsible for rural development. On the other hand, that responsibility is shared by the federal government and the provincial authorities, but they will reach those solutions only through co-operation.
I wonder if, at the present time, there are meetings between the federal Department of Agriculture and the provincial government of Quebec or Ontario about that

particular problem of marketing and market research.
What is the federal government exactly doing today to ensure that our dairy producers our cheese producers in Quebec and in the province of Ontario obtain the necessary outlets for their products? Does the federal government try as hard today to secure a stable market for our Canadian cheese producer as they did for the wheat producers?
I have nothing against the latter, and I am perfectly happy and in agreement with everything which is done to help them, but I would like to see the federal government jointly with the province of Quebec and the other provinces do the same for those other people.
I sometimes wonder whether it would not be opportune to set up a dairy board, similar to the wheat board, for instance, which would ensure that our dairy products meet national quality standards that are also acceptable internationally. Indeed this board might take joint action with the provinces and the dairy organizations with a view to securing a market for them, like the wheat board is doing at present by approaching every market in the world in its search for outlets.
We should have a similar organization which might dispose of our dairy farm products on every market in the world. I do not believe that this would be a prejudicial centralizing policy-far from it, as everything would be done in co-operation with the provincial governments, and more particularly with all organizations concerned. If this body were only like the wheat board which, to all ends and purposes, seems to be independent from the government as such. As this organization, as I say, was set up by the central government in agreement with the producers and wheat producing organizations, I believe that the same thing or something similar, might be repeated for the dairy farmers, which would provide them with the markets for which there is a great need.
They are now told: You are producing too much milk, you will have to do something else.
But has the assurance been previously given that another market could be found for the foodstuffs which they are asked to produce? Would it not be better, since a market must now be found for this new production, if the government itself, through some organization, found markets for the products for which they are equipped such as butter and cheese. I think that it is a serious problem.

The government would like them to give up part of their dairy production to produce something else. But was it anticipated that a market would nevertheless have to be found for that production? Besides, this transfer from one market or production to another is a burden for them, since they must now quit a production they developed at a loss, in order to reorganize in another line of production which in most cases requires a rather large investment for farmers who have been leading a precarious life for several years in a rather rough climate.
Relatively large funds have been placed at their disposal; but is it intended to get them into debt by urging them to turn to another type of production which, five years from now, will also be faced with a deteriorated market? And perhaps they will be asked then to change once more their line of production.
I think the thing should be thought out before urging our dairy farmers to diversify their production.
Indeed, allowance should be made for the fact that the population of Canada will not remain static, but will increase. And this dairy production, which may now have a temporary surplus, will not have a surplus forever.
Today, we say to dairy farmers: Reduce your production. Tomorrow or perhaps the day after tomorrow, we will have to beg them to increase their dairy production, in order to face the increased consumption due to the greater number of Canadian consumers.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude my remarks because I think that many other members want to speak on that subject. In my opinion, the federal government should now make it a point to co-operate with the provincial governments-and here I mean Quebec in particular-to secure markets for our present agricultural production before asking the farmers to engage in another kind of production for which we are not sure they will find markets or for which we are not ready to guarantee them markets.
That being said, Mr. Chairman, I resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the next few minutes to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who, a few minutes ago, made suggestions to the present government concerning the dairy industry.
I do not wish, today, to criticize the policy of the government but rather make a few recommendations to the Minister of Agriculture and to the agricultural stabilization
Supp ly-A griculture
board to help them find a way to assist the eastern farmers.
Mr. Chairman, it is well known that the dairy industry is the cornerstone of agriculture in eastern Canada, and in Quebec especially.
We know the dairy industry is the farmer's major source of income. A while ago, I was looking at the survey report tabled today by the Minister of Agriculture. That survey covered ten regions in the province of Quebec. In each, the dairy industry is at the top, providing farmers with the larger share of their income. Thus, 48 per cent of the income of farmers in those ten regions comes directly from the dairy industry and 16 per cent from the sales of cattle, which, in a way, is also part of the dairy industry.
If we are seeking ways to come to the assistance of eastern farmers, I think we have to know what will provide the farmer with the largest income, and that is the dairy industry.
In my opinion, the minister should pay a very special attention to this matter.
If the price of milk were to rise a little, the income of the farmers in the province of Quebec and eastern Canada would increase that much.
Some time ago a group of farmers marched on the provincial parliament. On that occasion, the minister of agriculture for the province of Quebec announced an increase of 20 cents per 100 pounds of milk. Farmers were immediately satisfied because they believed that this increase would apply to milk delivered to processing plants as well as to fluid milk. But they learned to their surprise that the increase was applicable only to fluid milk.
At the present time, Quebec farmers want to ask the federal government for an increase in order to raise their incomes. It is not only a certain group of farmers, but 71,000 dairy producers of that province.
Recently, I had a survey made in certain areas of the province of Quebec in order to ascertain the total number of pounds of milk sold by milk producers to their cooperatives. I should like to put on record the figures obtained in one area of the north shore, La Perade:	1,270 milk producers
shipped an average of 49,307 pounds of milk in 1961; in 1962, 1,235 milk producers shipped an average of 55,390 pounds of milk; in 1963, 1,222 milk producers shipped an average of 59,845 pounds of milk, still a slight increase. In such an area, milk is worth approximately

Supply-Agriculture
$3 per cwt.; this is not a very high income for those farmers who only rely on the dairy industry to support their family.
I now wish to quote the figures of the survey for 1963 only: 46 per cent of these 1,222 farmers shipped less than 50,000 pounds of milk, 22 per cent shipped between 50,000 and 75,000 pounds, 6 per cent shipped between
75.000	and 100,000 pounds and 13 per cent shipped between 100,000 and 150,000 pounds; finally, 3 per cent only shipped between
150.000	and 250,000 pounds. Consequently, if the federal government really desires to help farmers in eastern Canada it must take the necessary means to increase their income.
Last year, with its new dairy policy, the federal government saved the treasury about $11 million; this year, it will save the treasury between $4 and $5 million. Of course, the price paid to the producer for milk is somewhat the same as last year. In some places, this price is about 5 cents higher per cwt., in some other places, about 10 cents, but elsewhere it is 5 cents lower.
If the federal government saved the treasury $11 million last year and between $4 and $5 million this year, when the farmer receives about the same price, it is due to the fact that cheese is from 2 cents to 3 cents higher per pound, powdered milk is about 5 cents higher and finally, the demand for our dairy products is greater.
The suggestion I am making to the federal government is that this fall a special subsidy of 25 or 35 cents per cwt. of milk should be granted to eastern farmers up to a maximum of 100,000 pounds of milk. Such legislation would cost the federal government some $13 million, that is more or less the amount saved with the new farm policy passed last year and even then there would still be a few cents left over to give assistance in other fields.
If we figure that, in 1962, the subsidy of 25 cents per cwt. of milk paid to all eligible producers cost some $13 million and if, this coming fall, the government paid out to those eastern farmers a subsidy of about 35 cents per cwt. of milk for the first 100,000 pounds in order to increase their income, we would be, by the same token, giving assistance to most of the eastern farmers, because their average production is about 65,000 to 70,000 pounds shipped to processing plants.
If, in the province of Ontario, as was said by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton)-I was going to call him the minister of agriculture, because I anticipate that in a few months, he will be back at the head of

the Department of Agriculture-55.5 per cent of dairy producers have only 13 dairy cows, and 38.5 per cent have between 13 and 32, then I think that the situation is a little more serious in the province of Quebec. I am making this suggestion to the government in order that it may increase the income of those producers. And we can give good reasons to encourage the government to incur this $12 or $13 million expenditure early this fall. The Farmers' Advocate, in its June 1964 issue, quotes figures showing that in order to have an income of $3,000 per annum, a dairy producer should have 54 milch cows, with an average yield of 7,000 pounds of milk, the total of which amounts to 378,000 pounds of milk per annum, selling at $3.50 per cwt. or else 31 milch cows with an average production of 9,000 pounds, the total of which would represent 279,000 pounds selling at $3.50, or again, 22 milch cows, producing yearly an average of 11,000 pounds of milk for a total of 242,000 pounds of milk, which would earn $3,000 per annum, or still, 18 milch cows with an average yield of 13,000 pounds of milk, or a total of 234,000 pounds of milk which would bring in $3,000 per annum.
If we consider there are 55 per cent of the dairy producers in Ontario who keep less than 13 milch cows, and if we consider that in the province of Quebec, according to the data I have here, 7,484 dairy producers have obtained an average of 70,132 pounds of milk, evidently, their income is insufficient to allow them to meet their commitments. Now, if, in the province of Quebec for 70,000 producers the chief source of revenue is derived from the dairy industry, in my opinion, the government should focus its efforts on increasing income.
As a dairy farmer, I would say that the first 100,000 pounds of milk are necessarily the most expensive to produce and, as a matter of fact, they cost almost $3.50 per cwt. Keeping in mind that for each thousand dollars invested in dairy production it costs about $20 per milch cow, so that when the number is around 13, the income for the first
100,000	pounds of milk, the most expensive to produce, must be around $3.50 per cwt.
I remember that, in 1957-58, when I had the opportunity to visit the various areas of the province of Quebec and meet farmers, when the milk was worth about $2.50, $2.60 per cwt., I used to tell them: Milk ought to pay farmers an average price of $3 per cwt. We have now reached this average price of $3. At this time, it is not enough, we must go farther. In my opinion, we must not en-

courage just the big producers, the large organizations, so that they can keep on growing. We must help those who produce less than 100,000 pounds of milk.
I shall give an example. In the Granby area, in 1963, out of 1343 dairy farmers 68 per cent produced less than 100,000 pounds of milk per year, the average being 50,599 pounds.
In the Joliette area, in 1963, out of 736 producers, 79 per cent produced less than 100 pounds of milk a year, that is an average of 50,611 pounds a year. In the Bon-Con-seil area, my own area, in 1963, 57 per cent of the dairy farmers produced less than
100.000	pounds of milk, that is an average of 55,175 pounds of milk a year. In the La Perade area, on the north shore, in 1963, 84 per cent of the dairy farmers produced less than 100,000 pounds of milk, that is an average of 45,350 pounds a year. In the eastern townships, out of 400 producers, 57 per cent produced less than 100,000 pounds of milk, that is an average of 56,732 pounds a year.
In the area around Quebec city, including Megantic and Plessisville, out of 1,419 milk producers, 82 per cent produce less than
100.000	pounds of milk a year, or an average of 41,809 pounds. That is the situation in which our milk producers now find themselves.
We have small farms. Farmers have herds which are not too large, and mechanization is quite expensive. If the government really wants to help most farmers, it will have to implement this coming fall, or even sooner, the suggestion I put forth. And I am seriously warning the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), in short, the government, that Quebec farmers are getting ready to submit a request to the federal government and, if need be, to march on Ottawa. They have a right to do that.
If I were sitting on the other side of the house, I would advise government members to rouse public opinion throughout Canada, and more particularly in the cities. Our city dwellers should not think that farmers will always be the poor cousins in the Canadian economy. We should not forget that Ontario numbers about 70,000 or 72,000 producers, and the province of Quebec has about the same number. Those are people, families, human beings.
When did the government mind spending millions to help the miners? By following my suggestion, the government would spend a few million dollars to help thousands of people with inadequate income.
Supply-Agriculture
I make this suggestion, not because I want to criticize the policy the government enacted last year and which had its points. But I objected, though this policy had some good points, to the attempt which was made to save the federal treasury some money by every possible means, so as to be able to tell the city dwellers: We gave less to the farmers. That is not as it should be. Our fellow citizens who live in cities or towns should be made to understand that the farmer has a part to play, and that he should receive his rightful share of the national income. Indeed, if the farmer does not get an adequate income, he will move to the city and join the unemployed, or take the job of a person who is working and who would then become jobless in his turn.
Moreover, in some areas, families would have to receive social security allowances.
I should prefer the government to spend $12 or $15 million more in order to help directly the dairy farmers.
If the minister agrees to pay this additional grant next fall to farmers in Quebec, Ontario and the maritime provinces, up to 100,000 pounds of milk, I suggest that he should give this money directly to the farmers in two or three instalments. This would help increase the farmer's income. This will only be a temporary measure, since the appropriate long term measure is the one suggested earlier by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), that is, form a national dairy council which, I am sure, can do much for the dairy industry in Canada.
Just like the economists, we say there is at present a butter surplus. In fact, there are some 100 million pounds of butter in storage. Last year Canada produced 350 million pounds of butter, and approximately the same quantity was consumed. Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the passing of this item unduly but I should like to make a few remarks concerning crop insurance, since the minister was so kind as to allow us the opportunity of speaking on the subject on this item. As the years have progressed since the crop insurance bill was passed in 1959 I find that there is increasing interest in the subject across Canada. My own province of Manitoba in particular has pioneered the development of provincial crop insurance programs. Today a total of 6,170 farmers are covered in the six test areas that have been developed within the province, involving a total liability of over $14 million compared with just 2,500 farmers and a total liability of $4 million during the first year of operation, 1960-61.

I think this is a fairly clear indication that crop insurance in the province of Manitoba is receiving growing acceptance as a means of stabilizing farm yields. This is one point on which there seems to be confusion in the minds of a good many members whom I have heard discussing the subject in the house. First of all, I think it should be clearly understood that the crop insurance legislation introduced by the previous government in 1959 and passed by parliament was in effect enabling legislation which permitted provinces to set up their own crop insurance programs. It was one of those things mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday in speaking of provincial-federal cost sharing programs. Under this particular program the federal government does assume some responsibility, and some of the cost as far as administration and part of the premiums are concerned.
I think crop insurance should be designed to treat individual operators with similar risks in a similar fashion without unduly penalizing efficiency or subsidizing inefficiency. In other words, a crop insurance program to be effective must be actuarially sound, and it is on this basis that the Manitoba crop insurance corporation is proceeding and developing their program with some considerable success.
The matter raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle dealing with reinsurance is one that is of great importance to the province of Manitoba because they are very anxious to extend the provision of crop insurance across the entire province. But a year like 1961 and, again, a year like 1964 have caused them to proceed with a considerable amount of caution because of the risk that is involved and the necessity of having some form of reinsurance to fall back on, in the event of a disaster such as we are experiencing in parts of the west this year.
I am afraid there has been a tendency in some instances to emphasize crop insurance as a cure-all for all of the difficulties of agriculture. It is nothing of the kind. It is a part of an over-all farm program designed to minimize some of the variations in yield, and at its very best crop insurance can be no more than a device that levels out yields over a period of years. Obviously crop insurance cannot have any impact at all on the variability of income due to price fluctuations and for that reason the previous government when developing their farm program took into consideration the various things that contributed to agricultural instability and attempted to develop a program as national

in scope as possible, while at the same time taking into consideration regional problems that affect certain areas.
It is necessary therefore that the average production on a farm be such that it will provide the farmer with a decent income. Obviously crop insurance in those areas where average farm income over a period of years is so low that it does not provide sufficient income for the farmer is of little or no value to him. For that reason other programs must be developed to assist him. I have in mind particularly the provisions of the ARDA program under which a shift of emphasis in production will perhaps be more beneficial than the type of program we envisage under crop insurance. Paradoxically the areas that need crop insurance most can afford it least, because if it is to be based on the risk factor then of necessity the premiums are too high, and in many cases those areas where crop insurance is not required as much do not take advantage of it because the incidence of crop failure is so low that they do without it.
But in the greater part of Manitoba in particular crop insurance is the type of program that does provide that yield stability which contributes to the general well-being of the agricultural communities. It is not only the farmers of these communities who are affected. We recall that in the 'thirties the loss of income due to crop failures in those areas created a general depression among the business community. Farmers are unable to make purchases of equipment and pay necessary operating expenses if income is not available.
Again in 1961 we had an example of how crop losses due to weather conditions or conditions beyond the farmers' control can seriously affect other segments of the economy as well. For instance, in 1961 Manitoba farmers committed themselves to something like $117 million in cash operating expenses in the hope that the return from their crops would repay their expenses and provide them with a living for that year. Total net income for the year amounted to $64.6 million slightly over half of what it was the year before, and local businessmen as well as the farmers were very seriously affected. I happen to have visited those areas in Manitoba where crop insurance is in effect, and during the summer months it was easy to recognize the farmers who were covered by crop insurance because they were not nearly as worried as those who did not have coverage. On talking to businessmen in the area the same impression was created, that they were
Sup p ly-A griculture
optimistic in spite of the serious drought taking place at that time because so many of the farmers were covered by crop insurance.
In order to expand the operations of the Manitoba crop insurance corporation it is going to be necessary for the government to come up with the amending legislation at the earliest possible opportunity. I regret it will be delayed until fall because I know it is necessary in Manitoba to have this amendment to the legislation as quickly as possible, so that the corporation can proceed to accumulate the data and the necessary figures to determine what premiums and indemnities are to be paid in any given area.
The northern areas of Manitoba are suffering from rather severe drought, the central portions of the province are experiencing good crop conditions and the southeastern portion of the province, from which I come, is suffering severe flooding. From this one can see that the causes of crop failures are many and varied. Unfortunately the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, designed to offset the conditions of drought that existed during the thirties, does not adequately cover crop losses in the west today. There are areas where local flooding can create a great deal of difficulty for the farmers and the arrangements under P.F.R.A. could not possibly begin to cover the farmers affected. It is necessary, therefore, for them to seek aid elsewhere and if crop insurance were available all the farmers in the province could take advantage of its provisions and cover themselves adequately.
I recall that during the debate on the introduction of the bill in 1959 the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke at length on the subject of crop insurance, and criticized the then government because it did not take care of every ill, evil and contingency that could arise in agriculture. I only hope his opinions have been conveyed to the Minister of Agriculture so that he can take them into consideration.
I ask the minister to attempt to bring in this legislation at the earliest possible opportunity and thus facilitate the province of Manitoba and other provinces to proceed with the development of their crop insurance programs that will provide the type of stability farmers require these days when they have such high operating costs, and other costs that must be met from year to year.

I would like to ask the minister why, as Minister of Agriculture, he takes pleasure in reducing the income of the eastern farmers who devote themselves especially to the dairy industry. Mr. Chairman, it was my intention to speak on vote No. 15 and to deal particularly with supplementary payments pertaining to the sale of eggs and hogs under the stabilization board. My colleague the hon. member for Rosthern, has dealt with this matter but I should like to mention one thing that is of great concern to the producers of eggs and hogs in the west, the amendment

of the Agricultural Stabilization Act so that these payments will be made on a regional and also a semi-annual basis. We in the west have never received any deficiency payments in this regard and I do not think we will in the future unless something is done.
My remarks will pertain mostly to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act inasmuch as it will be made use of a great deal on the prairies this year, particularly in the area which at the present time is severely affected by drought conditions. I refer to the north central and northwest parts of Saskatchewan which at the present time are almost dried out. In these areas approximately 40 per cent of all the wheat planted in Saskatchewan is grown and approximately 60 per cent of all the oats and barley crops, and if we take this into consideration we can realize the severe conditions that the farmers are facing at the present time. The government has said that measures will be taken to alleviate the serious situation but in my opinion it is a case of too late and too little.
I think it came too little and too late- too late to the extent that had the minister taken into consideration the warnings given by the Leader of the Opposition, myself and some others, a number of the farmers would not be put in a position of having to sell some of their livestock. I say too little, because although some of the cattle will be put on community pastures the number of cattle involved in that is very small.
I would like to direct the minister's attention to the need for more community pastures, to be established under ARDA or other legislation. There are huge areas that could be converted into community pastures where farmers could place their cattle if in future they are faced with these drought conditions.
The situation is going to be very serious and many farmers will not have hay or other feed for their cattle. In these circumstances arrangements could be made to have the crops cut for hay before they are ready to be harvested, and provision should be made to have the areas in which this is done made eligible for payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Further, if the situation does not improve, measures should be taken to prevent feed from being exported out of the province so that it will be available to farmers during the winter period.
Yesterday the minister stated that he had seen these areas and therefore I shall not elaborate on this point. However, I would like to see him keep in close touch with the Saskatchewan department of agriculture and give all the attention he can to the situation.

Early in the session the minister announced a support or floor price of 47 cents a pound on flue cured tobacco. When the 1963 crop was sold the average price realized was 46.84 cents per pound, and I ask when will the support price be paid to these producers and whether the amount will be .16 cent per pound? Will it be paid to each individual grower or to the Ontario marketing board? If my figure of .16 cent per pound is correct this is going to mean less than $300,000, and this seems quite a small amount considering that the crop produces upwards of $400 million for the treasury through all forms of taxation. Further, will the flue cured tobacco growers in Quebec come under this support price?

With regard to the tobacco for which we provided the 47 cents support price, we have heard from the flue cured tobacco people and the average price for this tobacco was 49 cents a pound. In these circumstances there will be no deficiency payment.

I do not want to hold up this item too long as I wish to see the estimates go through this afternoon, and I shall do everything I can to expedite them. First, I want to thank the minister for having provided me with a copy of the increases and decreases in each vote because this has saved a good deal of time on asking questions.
The matter I want to speak about is one I raised in my opening remarks, namely that I am very deeply concerned about the dairy industry. I asked what inducements the minister was giving to the provincial governments and the farm organizations to encourage them to get together and form a single dairy organization. The reason I mentioned inducements was that we, as responsible members of parliament, want to take the load off the taxpayer that the stabilization act puts on him at present.
If you study the financial figures under the stabilization act you will find that for some years we support one industry and then for several years it will disappear as one of the items. The ultimate aim of the act should be not to have to pay anything, because when you don't have to pay anything it means every segment of the industry is able to look after itself.
At the moment the dairy industry is the sore spot and I am going to put forward, as briefly as I can, one or two suggestions which I hope the minister might take under consideration, if not for discussion at least to be aware that they should be considered. I make

Supply-Agriculture
these suggestions based on the fact that in my judgment the dairy industry, both at the producer level and at the processing level, is oriented toward the domestic market.
During the history of Canada the domestic market has been able to absorb the production from our dairy farms but in recent years, due to the rapid growth of technology and to the fact that more farmers wanted to raise their methods of living, we have a situation now when the productive capacity of our dairy farms is much greater than the Canadian market can absorb.
This problem can be met in two main directions. One is to move in with policies to encourage farmers at the marginal end of the scale in the dairy industry to move into other occupations or other types of farming. That is one road, and the other is to try and And, as was suggested by one of the hon. members to my left, an outlet for this production outside the country. The Canadian dairy industry and government officials tend to throw up their hands at the suggestion of finding relief in foreign markets. The reason for this is easily apparent. Price levels in Canada, the United States and most of the industrial countries of the world are so high for dairy products that we are not competitive with countries like New Zealand and Denmark which have a low cost type of product.
Because of this discrepancy in the price levels, and because of the advantages which efficient producers in Denmark and New Zealand enjoy and which we have not got, there is a tendency to say we cannot do anything about our dairy export markets. All we see ourselves doing is to give away our surpluses which are in storage at cut rate prices and let some individuals peddle them where they can with a depressing effect on world prices to the detriment of our good friends in Denmark and in New Zealand who are completely dependant on this type of market.
I rise at this time to challenge this type of thinking. I think that just because we are in a difficult situation with a price structure on the dairy side so different from the price structure of world market levels there is no need for despair. I think there are solutions. These solutions will not be easy but I think they can be reached not only in terms of our taking our industry in Canada outside into the markets of the world, but also by our realizing that at least a score of other countries are surplus in dairy products, and work with them because their problem is the same. In other words, a solution to the

dairy problem will not be reached only by agricultural support policies in this country. All you can do is twist and turn within the limits of the Canadian market, and if the present productive capacity of our dairy farms is producing 6 or 7 per cent above the demand, then the agricultural prices stabilization board works under great difficulty. But we might well realize the truth, that is that there are over a billion people in the world who desperately need protein products. I say "over a billion people" because I do not include the people of China. In my opinion the Chinese have been able to substitute protein derived from vegetables. But in the main the world demands proteins today from fish, from dairy products and from livestock products. The test is of course the difference in price, and the fact that in most of the countries where the need is so great they lack the ability to store these products and they do not have the ability to pay for them. These are the difficulties.
I would like to put forward some remarks or suggestions I made on September 17 last to a meeting at Stevens Point, Wisconsin to the creameries association. At that time there was not too much publicity attached to these remarks because other things were in the news. I was a little disappointed because I thought the time was right to move with our friends to the south on this point. Before I go into those remarks let me repeat that the problem of the dairy industry in the United States is almost identical with our own problem here. Their surplus runs at about 8 per cent as compared with 6 percent or 7 per cent here. They have a number of dairy farmers at the top level of efficiency who are doing well, but the great majority of their dairy farmers are in the same predicament as are the great majority of ours.
My suggestions to these men in the agriculture business were as follows: first, since the demand is mainly for protein food, that the dairy industry, including agri-business which handles dairy products, accept the possibility that there is a tremendous opportunity for expansion in the export market for dairy products that can satisfy the requirements of this new type of market. That is the first suggestion. Psychologically we should face the fact that if a billion people are hungry, we have the ability to produce and can get over the difficulties. That is the first suggestion: accept that philosophy. The second suggestion is that agri-business in North America join forces for a combined program of development of new

markets for farm produce. Why did I put that suggestion in? When you look at the businesses which handle and dispose of the products of American farms both here and in the United States, they are almost always the same businesses. Whether it is Swift here or in the United States, it is the same firm. They are working on this philosophy that the only market available for United States or Canadian farm products is in the United States or Canada. I say this philosophy is wrong in the year 1964 and we should ask this agri-business to accept some responsibility in helping to meet this situation.
The third suggestion I made was that government research in products suitable for handling, shipping, and storing for warm countries be accelerated. Already the United States department of agriculture has done a tremendous amount of work in this field. Already, here in Canada the department has done very good work in learning how to dry, store and handle varieties of different products. Our research and development in this respect are among the best in the world. I am simply suggesting in my third proposal that governments be encouraged to keep up this work and turn the results over to agribusiness. As a matter of fact, at the present time, in my opinion governments are ahead of business in this research work, and agribusiness in the United States and in Canada which for the most part is composed of the same firms, is delinquent in not making the best use of this research work which is available, so as to take Canadian and United States products to lands where they are needed at prices which the people can afford. I make that charge after due consideration.
The fourth recommendation I made was that the present efforts of the governments of Canada and the United States to achieve international commodity agreements be given increased impetus by the two governments calling a meeting of ministers of the dairy surplus countries, to help clear away the difficulties that are holding up present negotiations under the United Nations.
There are approximately 24 nations in the world which have surpluses of dairy products. Every one has the same problem as Canada. Discussions have been going on in the United Nations for a dairy commodity agreement. These discussions always founder on the point that these 20-odd nations have a higher price level domestically than the world price. I suggest this is not good enough. This type of price level can be met by international commodity agreement which makes
Supply-Agriculture
allowances in the form of quotas, and price levels within those quotas, to provide for the maintenance of a price which is necessary in our situation in Canada, the United States, Holland, the Scandinavian countries, Germany, and so on to give their producers fair returns. We should then be able to give to the world the advantage of our tremendous technology and ability to produce these protein products on our dairy farms, and allow these people in newly developing countries some chance of access to them.
I could examine this a little further by saying that in trying to get an international' commodity agreement Canada should always be first in the fight to help those newly developing nations get international commodity agreements for the products they sell. I hold those who are now in office and who are sitting on the treasury benches at the present time responsible for a lack of really gutty leadership on this question of international commodity agreements. Too easily did they stand aside and see the sugar agreement go down. If we had had an international sugar agreement fixing, say, 5 to 8 cents a pound for sugar at wholesale price levels we would be doubling the income of the people who produce sugar across the world, as compared with what they have received in the last 25-years without markedly increasing costs at home. In a favourable position of that kind they might well be able to buy from us the goods they need so desperately. So when it is said: We cannot make an agreement now because the price is too high, my answer is this-when the price is high is the time to start bargaining; if you start by assuming that you intend to give these people a fair price for their product they, in turn, will' be able to buy from us, thus taking a load off the shoulders of the taxpayer at home in connection with price support.
My fifth suggestion-I am not in the government now but I keep picking away at these problems-my fifth suggestion was that agri-business examine the multilateral trading techniques of the big international grain selling organizations to decide whether these companies could handle dairy products, or that similar types of organizations be set up for dairy products. I had in mind the tremendous productive capacity of the dairy industry in Canada and the United States and was wondering whether serious thought had ever been given by our producers to selling their goods abroad by using techniques which have been so successful in other fields, with what help the government can give.

Supply-Agriculture
I am suggesting we had better take a hard look at those international grain companies that are doing such a wonderful job for us today by selling the production of the wheat farms of the world. Many people think the wheat board sells Canadian wheat. Every time I have raised this question their eyebrows have gone up about an inch. Under the law the wheat board has the monopoly power to sell all the grain from western Canadian farms. But to be technically accurate, they turn that monopoly right over to agents of the board; so that the great bulk of Canadian grain is not actually sold by the Canadian wheat board at all-they simply give an agent a licence to sell the grain.
So there has developed in the grain marketing area of the world one of the most efficient operations the world has ever seen. There are four main international companies, Bunge, with headquarters in Rio de Janeiro; Cargill, with headquarters in Minneapolis; Continental, with headquarters in New York; and Dreyfus, with headquarters in Paris. These four great international grain companies not only handle wheat but any other type of cereal product. Why should they not, with all their vast machinery and know-how about the marketing opportunities for small amounts of 500 bushels of wheat today, or 5 million bushels tomorrow, consummate these sales in matters of seconds with their electronic communications apparatus? Why should they not consider taking over other products, such as butter oil? Why should they not take over anything that can be stored or shipped; anything that can be graded and put into storage? Everybody in this organization knows how much is available, at what price, and what grade. This type of organization has been developed in selling grain all over the world, and why cannot this knowledge be put to use to help the dairy industry?
If these international grain companies are already big enough in their own operations and do not want to go into other products, I think government leadership is necessary. The situation demands that we ask the dairy processors, who are so good and efficient, to handle our dairy products within Canada and the United States and to take on the big responsibility of helping our dairy industry. Government leadership should be provided to encourage them to get off their nice, plush seats and sell the products ofE the dairy farms of Canada and the United States all over the world. The reason I put these two countries together is that most of their dairy products are handled by the same companies.

The sixth suggestion I will leave for the moment because it would take too long to explain. I am sorry that I am rushing through these remarks, Mr. Chairman, but I want to help the minister get his estimates through. I want to conclude my remarks by saying that as I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska today I wondered how many in this house realized he was pioneering a new proposal in connection with the agricultural prices support board. He was bringing into the dairy industry a selective type of support, and he suggested that supports should be concentrated into the pockets of those who need them the most. The hon. member suggested, as I heard his speech through the translation system, that farmers producing up to 100,000 pounds of milk a year should be given the support of the agricultural prices support board; those that produced above that amount were big enough to get up on their own feet and find their own opportunities, which was not the case with the man whose production falls below this amount.
I do not know whether that suggestion will be workable, but I think it is the type of philosophy that was in the minds of the people who established the agricultural prices stabilization board, and his suggestion should be given serious consideration. This is the type of policy that we intend, when we take over the treasury benches, to put into effect. I suggest, further, that knowing the cost of producing milk, any government that does not aim to give producers of milk in every part of Canada a minimum price of $3.50 a hundred is not being fair to that segment of the Canadian people. We ask the provincial governments of this country to enact minimum wage laws providing a minimum wage of $1 an hour in most provinces. As the member for Nicolet-Yamaska made clear in the figures he quoted, even the man who produces 100,000 pounds-the maximum allowable under his suggestion-would only be guaranteed a gross income of $3,500 a year; and that would only mean a net income of about $1,500. Surely this is a right that farmers should expect in this country. I would say that not only will the Conservative party support that type of philosophy but we would like to move in this direction into other areas of our economy, such as the poorer areas of our cities. I cannot discuss this question here, but we would like to do the same thing with regard to other areas of our economy.
I would like to compliment the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska for putting that

proposal forward. I know the many hours of study he has put into this question and into the mathematics of what it will cost. With the knowledge I have of what he has done, I am prepared to support his proposal and go further and say that I think our target should be $3.50 a hundred for the production of milk in Canada, as a minimum.
I have said what I wanted to say, Mr. Chairman. There was another subject I intended to deal with, but I will just mention it briefly. I refer to the attitude of helplessness that comes over ministers at times when difficulties are put before them. We are now told that a milk program for our schools is impossible; that the provincial ministers do not think it is economic. This raises the whole question of dominion-provincial relations in this country. One of the questions I raised the other day in the house was as to whether the province of Quebec is going to expand its shared cost program under ARDA. The minister replied yes, that that is the type of thing that is a joint, constitutional responsibility of both the federal and provincial governments. I would suggest that this attitude should be spread; that each one of those joint sharing programs should be looked at by itself. If in the case of ARDA it is good to expand it, fine. But here we are dealing with a subject that is as equally important as the ARDA concept, namely the dairy support program. I would suggest that if you take the initiative away from the federal government to make proposals in connection with dairy support, the dairy problems in this country will never be solved. I say this because it is so easy for provincial ministers to slip back into the woodwork and disappear when this subject is raised. They do this because it is a tough subject. It is so easy for them to become chameleons and fit into any background.
I think the job of the federal minister is to bring these reluctant provincial ministers forward and say to them, "Sixty per cent of the farm population of your province is in dire need. We have to work together on this question". Let all the provincial treasurers and the Minister of Finance at Ottawa go back into the woodwork for a while. These are vital problems. If the Minister of Agriculture of Canada wants to make a name for himself and solve these problems of the dairy industry, he should bring these reluctant provincial ministers out into the open and tell them they have to share with him the responsibility of assisting this industry. They should go to the provincial governments and farm organizations and say, "We 20220-339

are prepared to help you this way, and this way, and this way, financially. But you have the constitutional power in many of these things, and therefore you must co-operate".
I think the farmers want an end to all this legal hair-splitting with regard to whose responsibility it is; they simply want action. One of the heaviest drains on the taxpayers of Canada is item 15 and the supplemen-taries that go along with it. I simply point out, Mr. Chairman, that the farmer does not want to bring his problems into this house and put heavier loads on the taxpayers under item 15; he wants a chance to solve his problems by his own efforts. But he has to have the leadership not only of the federal minister but of the provincial ministers. I do not know how far I will get in making these proposals but I do know that I intend to keep working for them.

I do not intend to hold up the committee because I should like to see this estimate passed, but I do want to say a few words on administration. I have been very patient with the minister ever since he took over his portfolio. One could not expect a minister after years of being so conservative to be very liberal in this short space of time. And he has not been getting any help from his colleagues, which is very necessary if he intends to do anything or to get anywhere. I have worked with his officials and I find them fine fellows to work with, but they have to have direction from the government and they cannot go ahead without direction. The minister is not giving them sufficient direction to do the things we expect him to do.
To prove my point I should like to show you how interested is the Liberal government in agriculture. We have an agricultural committee of which I have been a member for the last 24 years. The other day we sat for 35 minutes before we could get a quorum. Half of the Conservative members were ready to proceed, but we waited 35 minutes for a quorum. Then at the best we had only four Liberals sitting on the committee. The meeting was called for 9.30 and we sat there until 12.30 and at no time were more than four Liberal members present. So, Mr. Chairman, you cannot expect the minister to do everything for the country when he has no backing from his own side of the house.
I would suggest to those Liberal members of the agriculture committee that if they do not understand anything about agriculture let them go to the committee where they will find out a few things. It is essential this

Supply-Agriculture
committee have a quorum, and I do not think it is fair to its members to have to sit there for 35 minutes-sometimes it is 40 minutes -waiting for a quorum.
Would the hon. member permit a question. In the banking and commerce committee the last time it met there was only one Conservative there, who showed up for about 10 minutes.

Since the hon. member raises that, yesterday a meeting of the public accounts was called. It is chaired by a Conservative to make it non-political. We sat there for 35 minutes and only one Grit came along. Eventually we adjourned and did not have a meeting at all. These officials who appear are called to give the committee guidance, yet hon. members opposite do not think it important enough to attend. I have no intention of criticizing the minister on these estimates; we want to get them through. I only rose in my place to try and help him as much as I can, if he will try to help himself.

40. Administration, operation and maintenance including Canada's fee for membership in the office international des epizooties, and authority, notwithstanding the Financial Administration Act, to spend revenue received during the year from packers requiring special services, $11,954,900.

Mr. Chairman, I did not want to take up too much time on this item but there is one matter I want to mention in connection with the operation of the health of animals division. I do not mean this to be a criticism of the officials of the branch of this department; Dr. Wells and his staff are doing a very commendable job of carrying out the policies of the administration of this department. However, during the last year a matter was drawn to my attention which I should like to raise with the minister at this time. It is in connection with poultry evisceration stations and the inspection of poultry processed through these evisceration stations.
I note from a reply to a question which I placed on the order paper on October 1 last that the percentages of the number of condemned birds going through these plants is increasing. Logically it is expected that this would be the case if the number of birds being processed was increasing as well. However, I find that the number of condemned birds is increasing out of proportion to the increase in the number of birds being processed.
On investigating I discovered that some of the farmers in my area are disturbed about

this matter. The situation is simply that they feel they own the birds. They have no contract for sale when the birds are brought into the evisceration plant, yet in some cases a fairly substantial percentage of these birds are condemned and are simply taken out of the farmers' hands. These farmers have paid for the cost of raising the birds, and arbitrarily they are being taken away from them and sent to the rendering plants. In some cases I understand the evisceration plants are selling the birds to the rendering plants at a profit, the farmer receiving nothing.
I am fully conversant with the problem of the health of animals division in ensuring that the consuming public are supplied with high quality meat. I will not go into details about this matter because I have had experience in this field, but here is a principle which should be looked into. I asked the minister whether he would direct his officials to give attention to this particular problem so as to ensure that, in cases where a farmer feels he has been unduly penalized as a result of a large number of his birds being condemned and taken away from him and sold by the evisceration plant at a profit, there should be some return given to the farmer for these birds. I was wondering whether the minister could comment on that or would look into the matter for me.
Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to look into this; and I should like to speak to the hon. member privately with regard to the locations where these problems exist.

In view of the fact that this item concerns ARDA and there has been a split in the duties of the Minister of Agriculture, and a new department is going to be formed relating to ARDA and forestry, I wonder if we could get some sort of statement of philosophy from the new minister who is going to be looking after ARDA and forestry? What does he intend to do with this legislation? I would think a statement could be made in four or five minutes. We would not expect him to make a lengthy statement, but let us hear what his thinking is on ARDA in a general way.

Mr. Chairman, as members of the house know, government order No. 60 will be called this fall to introduce the new department of forestry and rural development. I then hope, at the resolution stage, to make a lengthy declaration on ARDA, rural development and the conditions in rural areas. I shall be pleased, however, to make a few remarks today on how the program is working and what we intend to do with the program.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle will recall with great pleasure that he had the honour of introducing this legislation into the House of Commons. As I have said here in the house and outside, it was probably one of the best pieces of legislation the previous government introduced. I have commended him for this. This is a joint federal-provincial program which is, in a way, in the experimental stage. It has been going on for three years. We have projects in all the provinces of Canada. We have signed general agreements and special agreements with all the provinces. I have announced that I hope at the end of August or early September, to call a federal-provincial conference of the ministers responsible for ARDA to review the existing agreements, with a view to signing new agreements that would begin on April 1, 1965 for a number of years.
