Supply-Agriculture
I have been visiting all the provinces of Canada and discussing all the problems related to ARDA with the ministers. There is a general consensus that this is an excellent program and there is a great future for it. My basic philosophy on ARDA is rather simple. If I could express it in a few words, I would say that I feel this law is entirely directed toward the low income people, the low income regions in rural areas. We have to do everything we can to eliminate poverty in the rural areas. It is not only an agricultural program, but it is a program to look after all resources in the rural areas-agriculture, forestry, fishing, tourism, small industries-and we have to devise ways and means of improving the living conditions of the people in the rural areas, people who have a right to as good a living as the people in urban areas.
This will mean new methods of co-ordinating the services of provincial governments and the federal government, co-ordination at the regional level and at the national level, by means of new experiments in government. It is for this reason the meeting we will have this fall to review the agreements is so important. We are having meetings with the province of Quebec about this rural development of the region of the lower St. Lawrence, about which I have talked in the house and about which members of the house received a folder last week giving them much information. I am very proud to be responsible for the implementation of this law which to me is a wonderful piece of legislation and I hope members will support it as they have supported it in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I noticed and also read in the newspapers that the Quebec regions where ARDA will be applied are as follows: Gaspe, Iles-de-la-Madeleine, represented by the minister, and Abitibi, represented by hon. Mr. Courcy, minister of agriculture in the Quebec government. I have no objection to the fact that those regions, which need help, will benefit from ARDA and to the fact that the two ministers concerned try to help their own people first. I do not have any objection to that, but I would not like the authorities concerned to show any discrimination in the application of that act.
The areas represented by the members of the government should not be the only ones to benefit under the ARDA program; others also need assistance, such as the regions of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and Ber-thier-Maskinongi-Delanaudiere, for example,

Supply-Agriculture
or the one represented by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), and others.
I should like to ask the minister on what basis he selects the areas which are to benefit under the ARDA program? Why have we neglected to apply the act to the counties of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere where a large part of the population needs as much assistance, under this program, as the region of lles-de-la-Madeleine or that represented by the Quebec minister of agriculture?
As I said before, I have no objection if those areas benefit from it. But other areas represented by members not on the government side, surely have the right to see that their people also benefit from that legislation.
The area which I represent, namely Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm-especially the northern part of the Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm riding-and also the Berthier-Mas-kinonge-Delanaudiere area are faced with serious economic problems. There is in those areas of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, a well organized economic planning board which, for some months, has attempted to have a portion of that area come under ARDA.
I wonder why the minister declines to put that area as well as some other areas such as that of Brome-Missisquoi, or that part of the province, under ARDA.
I should be very pleased if the minister would tell the house on what basis he chose the areas where ARDA is to be applied. Is it a political criterion? He should tell us. If it is an economic criterion, he should tell us also.
I am astonished to see that the first areas where ARDA is applied are those areas represented by the two ministers I have mentioned above, the federal Minister of Forestry and the minister of agriculture for Quebec.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, I must say this: Mr. Courcy, minister of agriculture in the Quebec government, attacked me unfairly in the Quebec legislature during the present session. He said that the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, when he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of agriculture, tried to mislead the farmers by telling them: "Submit your accounts to the government and they will be paid."
Mr. Chairman, I challenge the provincial minister of agriculture to prove this statement. I never said such a thing. Therefore I ask the provincial minister of agriculture to show no discrimination in the selection of

areas for the application of ARDA and to help equally the areas not represented by government members.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that my hon. friend will believe me when I say that I had nothing to do with the selection of the nine areas of the lower St. Lawrence and Abitibi which would benefit from the ARDA program in the province of Quebec.
This procedure began last year when I was not yet a minister, as my hon. friend knows. Moreover, it is the provincial minister of agriculture who undertakes to propose to the federal government the development of projects under ARDA. The federal government has nothing to do with the selection of development areas or still with the submission of practical projects of drainage, soil conservation or community pastures.
I think my hon. friend is somewhat confused. At present, five groups of projects are foreseen under ARDA and so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, hon. Mr. Courcy stated at Mont Joli, last Saturday, that for some time there will be only two rural development areas, namely the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe area and the Abitibi area. I believe I pointed that out to my hon. friend yesterday. Those two areas were designated exclusively on the basis of economic considerations and the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) is familiar enough with the province of Quebec to know that, in those rural areas, the level of income of many families is the lowest in the province. That is why the provincial government decided to develop first of all these two areas. The fact that Mr. Courcy is member for Abitibi and that the present speaker is member for the constituency of les lles-de-la-Madeleine is irrelevant for, in my case, this happened long before my appointment.
This does not mean that because there are only two designated areas, no other projects will be submitted by the province of Quebec; in fact, the reverse is true. Up to now, we had more than 117 projects submitted by the province of Quebec, representing a total amount of $6 million. Moreover, other projects are under study; projects for the province of Quebec concern drainage and very few have anything to do with development programs such as I have just mentioned. I wish my hon. friend knew there is no limitation, except in the designation of areas.
The Joliette area, and the other areas in need of ARDA, will continue to benefit from it, but the initiative rests with the provincial

government. It is not for the federal government to decide what should be done. According to the terms of the agreement between the federal government and the provincial governments, it belongs to the provinces to take the initiative, since they are responsible for the administration of ARDA.
My hon. friend should believe when I declared that neither hon. Mr. Courcy nor myself interfered to obtain the designation of the areas we represent.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to add a few words to what the minister has said-

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words concerning ARDA to the new Minister of Forestry who is in charge of administering the program. We are not satisfied with the number of projects that have been started in western Canada, particularly in Alberta and above all in the southern part of Alberta. I read the report prepared for the minister's office and to me it connotes that there is nothing but a lot of sidetracking going on. In other words, what has been done in most cases is to sidetrack the ARDA program and, if possible, shift matters to the P.F.R.A. administration which is under the Minister of Agriculture.
Why has scarcely nothing taken place? Because the federal government will be expected to pay the full shot under P.F.R.A. whereas under the ARDA program it would be a co-operative venture with a sharing of costs with the provinces and local governments. There is something very seriously wrong with the set-up, with the action we are getting and the number of projects that

are being undertaken. I say to the minister that even with all the projects he has okayed he has not scratched the surface. This inaction should be corrected. He must learn that he cannot sit in a law office in Montreal and expect to get results under this program by leaving all of the initiative to the provinces.
I know that agreements of understanding have been reached with the provinces, as the minister has just indicated, but the present situation was not contemplated when the house passed the act. There was supposed to be aggressive initiative on the part of the minister in charge of administering ARDA. It is one act which, if properly administered, could do more to develop this country than any other law on the statute books of Canada.
The minister has said that he believes it is a good act. Let me tell him that it is not being administered properly. I suggest to him that he take another look at the situation. I suggest that he clear up some of the difficulties, some of the strife between P.F.R.A. and ARDA and do so right in the provinces so that we will get some action in those dry areas of western Canada along the Rocky mountains which are begging and hoping to have surveys made and an active program implemented under ARDA.

Mr. Chairman, I will take only a couple of minutes to say that I was very pleased with the minister's brief statement with respect to rural rehabilitation and to note in his statement that there is a continuity of spirit and philosophy with respect to rural rehabilitation. I must say I thought it was sporting of him to give credit to the former minister for having introduced this very useful legislation, which has a great potential if we can get co-operation among the federal government, the provinces and the local people. I think the foundation of success for this program lies in co-operation among all levels of government, the organizations involved and the people themselves. This group will look forward to the introduction of the legislation that the minister mentioned and to his statement with respect to the policy in connection with the further expansion of this program.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few more questions to ask. I can assure the minister that if he agrees to postpone the consideration of his estimates till the next sitting, the vote will be passed in half an hour or three quarters of an hour. However, the

Mr. Chairman, if I had not been interrupted so often a while ago, I am convinced that we would have made more progress and that the vote under consideration would have been passed.
When the Minister of Forestry was an ordinary member, he approached the Quebec authorities-and I do not criticize him for that-in order that the area of lles-de-la-Madeleine might be included in the ARDA program, and I commend him for this initiative.
I know for a fact that the economic council for the riding of Montcalm was one of the first public bodies of the country, more especially in the province of Quebec, to make strong representations to the federal Department of Agriculture so that that area of our province might come under ARDA. However, I wonder why the provincial minister of agriculture, whose responsibilities it is to select the areas, ignored the

Montcalm riding which surely deserves careful attention.
I know also that the minister is on excellent terms with the Quebec authorities, and I would like ARDA to be used so as to truly help the farm people in those regions where the act will be applied.
On the other hand, I would not like that act to be used for patronage purposes, because I hear that is being done now. As a matter of fact, according to some letters I have received, the people who do work under ARDA are carefully selected.
Consequently, and knowing that the minister is not directly responsible for the application of ARDA in the provinces, I ask him to watch very closely what is going on, so that the act may be applied fairly and in the public interest.
I wonder if, without going to any trouble, the Minister of Forestry could not ask the Quebec authorities to make a study on tourism in part of the region of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and Berthier-Maskinonge so that it may benefit from ARDA?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member's proposal is contrary to the agreements we have signed not only with the province of Quebec but with the other provinces of Canada. Initiatives must come from the province itself and I suggest to my hon. friend to ask the regional authorities concerned to write the Quebec minister of agriculture to submit their project.
The act forbids me to interfere in that field and even if I wanted to oblige, I could not do so, because I would not want to interfere in fields which come strictly under the provincial government.
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his co-operation.

I had not intended to intervene because I think there has been a great deal of discussion on the agriculture estimates, but this item warrants some comment. The discussion which has just taken place is an indication of where the problem lies. The ARDA program has been talked about as a major, long term solution to most of the depressed agricultural communities but we are now seeing, and this has become more clear since the Liberals took office, that ARDA is to be provincial in scope and if a province does not want to make a request for a particular project then the federal government can do nothing about it. This is not what

we originally agreed to on the ARDA program.
We originally agreed that the program would be administered by the provinces, but if we find that the provinces fail to take advantage of it then we shall have to do something ourselves. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, the patronage machine in the province of Ontario is much more raw than the one in Quebec, where it is an accepted thing. We in Ontario are finding patronage is a very vile and distasteful thing, but it is being used to a great extent in the ARDA program. We are seeing patronage in Ontario today never seen in that province before, and probably only duplicated by some of the western agricultural programs undertaken many years ago.
When the minister made his statement he was very fair in saying he hoped this program would have a long term application, and I know he is not responsible for all of the abuses that take place. I am also aware of the arrangements that have to be made because of the jurisdiction of the provinces; but let us not tell the farmer we are going to solve all his problems with ARDA if we are not prepared to interfere with some of the little bourgeoisie arrangements made in some Of the townships, areas and ridings.
What the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm was really saying was, "Please, Mr. Minister, because I have spoken about this don't hold it against me, or at least give my people an opportunity to have something under ARDA." I do not agree with that. If we cannot get a fair and reasonable program applicable all across the nation without a member of parliament having to get up and beg, then we do not want it as a solution.
Farmers are not beggars. It is not the agricultural section of our section of our nation which got itself into the predicament it is in. It is because the nation has not been able to meet the change of the times. ARDA was developed to meet this change, and surely people should not be made to beg for it in particular areas.
Without even knowing the facts I am certain, just because the minister is who he is, that is not why a program was carried out in a particular county in Quebec; but I feel the provinces themselves are using ARDA for their own ends and not for the ends upon which we as a national government decided.
I agree with what the minister said, that what we want to do is pick out all the areas where income is very low and where a
Supply-Agriculture
transition out of agriculture is probably the solution. He mentioned the fact that some of this would be into the tourist industry, some into the forest industry and some into other fields of agriculture where redevelopment would be taking place. I say we have to begin this with a survey. We have to assess the needs. We have to apply the money to the areas that need it most, and not decide because of the political advantage of using it in certain areas.
The provinces will always use ARDA for their own ends because it is a handout, and for this reason I urge that the federal government stay very strongly in this field. Instead of waiting for proposals from the provinces the federal government will have to point out which proposals will be acceptable to it and get the provinces to make formal request for them.
According to the minister's own words he is going to carry on ARDA in the direction which the former minister who introduced it had in mind, namely in the direction of being a long range solution for depressed agricultural communities. But this cannot be done if we are going to give in all the time to the whims and wishes of the various provincial governments. We shall have to assess the over-all agricultural potential of Canada and the federal government will have to give the leadership in this field. If we have not got the power to do this now, then let us make an arrangement with the provinces whereby we can get that power.
In the province of Quebec they did not have a trans-Canada highway. It was not our fault in the rest of Canada; it was their fault. They did not take advantage of the provisions which had been made. We at least supplied a program of a type they could have taken part in. I suggest we do this with regard to ARDA. We should make proposals which will apply to all the provinces, to all the depressed agricultural areas, and if the provinces want to take advantage of them there should be no discrimination used in selecting the riding in which work is being done-that is, on political ground. Anything less will not be acceptable to the agricultural community of Canada.
I think the minister will make a great contribution-and certainly the minister who preceded him did not make this sort of contribution-if he would give real leadership in this field of ARDA, designed to relieve depressed agricultural areas. I believe ARDA can provide a solution to many of the problems faced by our agricultural community

Supply-Agriculture
When you find people earning an income of only $600 or $700 a year, then obviously the process being followed is not the correct one for that area.
I hope that the minister when he speaks on this subject will be prepared to tell us what he is ready to offer to the provinces under this plan and what leadership he intends to give. I say this because I am getting damned tired of waiting for the provinces to give a lead in this direction. What they have done so far does not, in my opinion, come anywhere near to meeting the need which ARDA was designed to satisfy.

The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has cast a lot of doubt on what is actually happening in connection with this program. I do not agree with him, I must say.
Could the minister tell us whether within the last six, eight or ten months liaison has been taking place with the various ministers of agriculture in other provinces with regard to ARDA. Perhaps at the same time he could tell us whether he feels ARDA is working. Perhaps he would indicate, too, whether it is not working on the highest political level, as suggested by the previous speaker. I have cause to believe that in my own province it is working, and I would not like to think the situation was different elsewhere in Canada. Perhaps the minister could set at rest whatever fears some may have.

I am pleased to inform the committee that I have tried to give the leadership for which the hon. member for Timiskaming asked. I was made responsible for ARDA on March 5 and between March 17 and May 30 I visited every one of the ten provinces. I have had discussions with the ministers and civil servants responsible for ARDA in each province. We have exchanged views and we are now preparing our submissions for a conference which I hope to be able to call at the end of August or early in September with a view to redefining, in a way, the scope of the program and the methods of its implementation.
In the last four or five months there has been a tremendous increase in the number of projects submitted by the provinces and, as the law stands now, the initiative in terms of projects has to come from the provinces. This is not the result of any recent change. It was the law when this legislation was passed by parliament. This is a joint federal-provincial program and I have no authority

to change it in this respect. It is working well, generally speaking, and there is great interest in the provinces about ARDA. However, this is still a very new concept. Originally it was thought of as being strictly an agricultural program, but it was found that you could not solve the problems of the rural areas by taking only an agricultural approach. It had to be extended to forestry, mining, fishing, tourism and so on. There has been over the years an extension of the program. This is in line with the provisions of the original law passed in 1961. It is true there have been problems of adjustment and administration. I might point out that the federal government has nothing to do with the administration at the provincial level. If here and there there are political considerations affecting decisions, as the hon. member suggested, it is not our responsibility. We have nothing to do with it, and I would be the first to regret it. If there were anything I could do to help in any such cases I would certainly bring them to the attention of the responsible minister. I am sure the ministers responsible are probably not aware of them and that they would be the first to take steps to correct such situations.
There has been great interest in ARDA in the last few months. As a result of the visits made to the provinces and with the passage of time, the provinces are getting to know how to work with this new plan. Nobody is to blame for what has happened in the past. It has taken time for an understanding of ARDA to develop in all the provinces.

I gather from the minister's statement that he is satisfied generally with the way things are going. He mentioned the calling of a conference. Does he feel any important changes will be made? He says be believes a redefinition of the aims and objects of ARDA is needed. Does he believe these changes will depart to any great extent from the original concept?

I have stated in the house many times in answer to questions that the agreements between the provinces and the federal government come to an end on March 31, 1965, and with a view to re-negotiating these agreements we shall call a meeting of the provinces with the federal government. The provinces have already proposed many changes and we also have many changes to propose to the actual agreements. We do not know if the changes we wish to propose will necessitate amendments to the actual law. We are working on this now. But we are

hoping that there will be no need for amendments to the law. We hope to be able to bring about these changes-there will probably be 15 or 20 important ones-by changes in the agreements only, and these we are preparing now, here in Ottawa.
We are satisfied with the law in the sense that it has done good, but there are a number of improvements which could be brought about and this will be done when we meet with the provinces at the end of August or early in September.

There are one or two additional points I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Perhaps through no fault of his own but through his lack of understanding of the various regions of Canada he seems to have in the back of his mind the idea of a depressed area, a backward area-the problems which are now present in Quebec-and is using this as a touchstone before embarking upon ARDA projects.
This should not be so, because we have no, or very few, such areas in western Canada. We do have a lot of virgin territory. We have the Rocky mountain area, with streams which need to be controlled by dams and other structures so as to generate energy and make it possible to bring in industry. The power of those streams could be harnessed so that industry could be brought into being. It is needs of this kind which ARDA programs in the west should explore and satisfy.
If the hon. gentleman intends to wait until we find in the west situations such as exist in certain parts of Ontario and Quebec there will never be anything done under ARDA in western Canada. I am wondering whether this attitude in the mind of the minister and of others in the government is responsible for the inactivity which has been shown under this program in western Canada.
I like some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming and I agree with some of them wholeheartedly. I would suggest again to the minister that he take another look at the objectives to which he' should be giving consideration, and that he should spread the action of this program throughout all Canada, including western Canada, and not confine it to the depressed areas.

If I might reply to the hon. member, I would suggest he look at the figures. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta had $17 million worth of projects approved up to April 13. So they certainly had their 20220-340
Supply-Agriculture
share. When I said earlier in my opening remarks that I felt ARDA should be concentrated mainly in low income areas, to assist low income people, I did not mean that this should be exclusively the case, but mainly, because it is in these areas that there is the greatest need. There are many other agricultural measures enacted by the federal government and the provincial governments which have a bearing on problems existing in the rural areas, but this program seems to be mainly oriented to assisting people in low income areas. It does not exclude other responsibilities that are contained in our law; but I think this is the intention behind the measure, namely to try to eliminate poverty in rural areas.
We do not have a concentration of low income people all over the country; they are mainly concentrated in eastern Canada. There are low income areas in all the provinces, but in these areas there are not as many people affected as there are in the east, in Quebec and the maritimes.

Mr. Chairman, did the minister read that section of ARDA, which deals with rural development, industrialization, and so on? If he had, and had considered the interpretation of what is contained therein, he would not have made the statements he has just made; he would have a broader concept of the functions of ARDA.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in listening to the minister say he had visited all the ten provinces in order to discuss with them problems connected with ARDA. I am sure the minister is-and if he is not, he should be-aware of the agricultural and resource potential of all kinds above the 60th parallel in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, with all sorts of timber resources and livestock potential in the agricultural field there, and feed grain possibilities. There is also this potential in the Mackenzie. The very fact that experimental farms have been established in both these areas in itself indicates the agricultural potential of the two areas concerned. I am not confining my remarks to the agricultural potential only, but also to the general resource potential that exists in this part of the country.
I wonder whether the minister is going to display any initiative and visit the rest of Canada apart from the ten provinces he said he has visited, and is going to take a journey north to see for himself how ARDA can be applied in this vast area of Canada which has

very great potential indeed which in the ultimate will result, if proper development policies are adopted to the lasting benefit of all Canadians. It is their land; they are their resources; and it is an area which is deserving of the very concentrated attention of not only the minister responsible for ARDA but of all ministers having a direct responsibility in resource development in the north, where they do not have that responsibility in the provinces. I wonder if the minister could just for a moment explain how he intends to apply ARDA in the north, what his plans are for a possible visit there, and the like.
I shall be pleased to visit the Yukon and Northwest Territories, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I think I would be remiss in my duty if I did not thank hon. members for the consideration they have given the agriculture estimates and ARDA. We do appreciate their interest and approval.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF PENALTIES UNDER UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, as the explanatory note suggests, is presented in view of Canada's commitment under the United Nations convention on the crime of genocide. This convention was tabled in the House of Commons on March 2, 1950, and in the Senate on March 14 of the same year. It was approved by resolution of the house on March 21, 1952, and by resolution of the Senate on March 27 of the same year. The instrument of ratification was deposited with the United Nations on September 3, 1952, and the convention came into force on December 2 of the same year. This convention binds the contracting states to pass the necessary legislation to give effect to its provisions, especially to provide effective penalties. The intention of this bill, among other things, is to discharge Canada's obligations to the United Nations. Genocide is defined in the bill as follows:
Every one who, with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group as such, kills a member of the group, is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be sentenced to death for genocide.
The second clause of the bill deals with incitement to genocide; the third clause deals with group libel. It may be said that the present laws with respect to genocide-I am not now dealing with the question of group libel-are adequate; in other words, there is a section of the Criminal Code dealing with capital punishment. I submit that the present provisions do not fully encompass what is intended by the crime of genocide. First of all, and aside from the moral effect of Canada subscribing to a law under the United Nations convention, there is a possibility-and I for one would support the proposition-that eventually our society will reach that plateau of civilization where it will abolish capital punishment. However, there are sections of the Criminal Code prescribing capital punishment which will not be abolished for such crimes as treason, and should not be abolished, because of the enormity of the crime, for the crime of genocide. So that if genocide were to be declared an offence under our law and capital punishment abolished in the future, it would still be retained for the crime of genocide.
With regard to treason, section 46(l)(a) of the Criminal Code says:
Everyone commits treason who in Canada (a) kills or attempts to kill Her Majesty, or does her

any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, maims or wounds her, or imprisons or restrains her-
Here is a section in the Criminal Code which makes a provision with respect to capital punishment which is otherwise provided for in the Criminal Code, and it is this sort of thing which this bill envisages in making genocide a capital offence in spite of the provisions of capital murder.
I should also like to put on record a resolution adopted by the United Nations general assembly on November 21, 1963, which I believe was one day prior to the assassination of President Kennedy. Article 9, paragraph 1 of this resolution, to which Canada subscribed, says:
All propaganda and organizations based on ideas or theories of superiority of one race or group of persons of one colour or ethnic origin with a view to justifying or promoting racial discrimination in any form shall be severely condemned.
Paragraph 2 says:
All incitement to or acts of violence, whether by individuals or organizations, against any race or group of persons of another colour or ethnic origin shall be considered an offence against society and punishable under law.
In order to put into effect the purposes and principles of the present declaration, all states shall take immediate and positive measures, including legislative and other measures, to prosecute and/or outlaw organizations which promote or incite to racial discrimination, or incite to or use violence for purposes of discrimination based on race, colour or ethnic origin.
Clause 3 of this bill provides for a group libel law. I inserted that provision in the bill because I maintain that group libel is the seed of genocide. Genocide can only be committed by a government; it cannot be committed by individuals. The only way a government can come into power to a point where it could commit genocide is by the systematic use of propaganda to defame and libel minority groups, as we have seen.
The libel under our law of an individual, which is provided for by definition in section 248 of the Criminal Code states that:
A defamatory libel is matter published, without lawful justification or excuse, that is likely to injure the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or that is designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published.
One of the defences against defamatory libel of an individual is provided for in section 261 of the Criminal Code, which states:
No person shall be deemed to publish a defamatory libel where he proves that the publication of the defamatory matter in the manner in which it was published was for the public benefit at the 20220-340J
Genocide
time when it was published and that the matter itself was true.
This section refers to individuals. There is no provision in the Criminal Code with respect to an attack on an ethnic, national or religious group as such. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that you can never make a statement, an all-embracing, blanket statement, against an ethnic or religious group which is libellous and which can be true. It is impossible to make a libellous statement which can be true against an entire group of people. You might be able to do so in the case of an individual but you cannot make a true statement which is libellous against an entire group of people.
Oddly enough, while the Criminal Code does not provide for group libel it does provide for false advertisement in business. Section 306, which is the section protecting competitors in business, reads as follows:
Everyone who publishes or causes to be published an advertisement containing a statement that purports to be a statement of fact but that is untrue, deceptive or misleading or is intentionally so worded or arranged that it is deceptive or misleading, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years, if the advertisement is published.
(a)	to promote, directly or indirectly, the sale or disposal of property or any interest therein, or
(b)	to promote a business or commercial interest.
An example of that might well be this. A person who manufactures soap could not make the blanket statement that the soap manufactured by his competitors is poisonous and should not be used, because under section 306 of the Criminal Code he could be prosecuted and might well face imprisonment for five years. Yet the same individual could make any sort of blanket statement which was defamatory and libellous against a group of human beings and escape scot-free. And not only would he escape scot-free but he would actually be protected by our law. I think there is something wrong with the laws of this country when business enterprises and products of business can be protected but human rights cannot.
Now, the disseminators of hate and hate propaganda are persons who are already consumed by their hatred. They are people who are already destroyed mentally and are seeking to destroy other people. They are actually using freedom to destroy freedom. There was an interesting symposium held in the United States at the Cleveland-Marshall law school of Baldwin-Wallace college. I should like to quote some of the statements made in that symposium. One of those who

Genocide
took part was Mr. Justice Clark of the supreme court of the United States. I am quoting from volume 13, No. 1, January 1964, the issue of the law review of that university. Judge Clark said:
Group libel statutes "represent of commendable desire to reduce sinister abuses of our freedom of expression-abuses which I have had occasion to learn can tear apart a society, brutalize its dominant element and persecute even to extermination, its minorities".
Going further, the judge stated:
Even professional defamers are, today, insulated and protected by our laws from civil liability, as long as their words or actions remain "wholesale" defamation and do not single out specific individuals or numerically small groups.
In the same issue in the summation of the symposium it is stated:
It is obvious that the constitution of the United States and the common sense of the American people must prevent similar excesses in this country. And we feel a chill of foreboding as we think of recent riots in Alabama, culminating in the bombing of a Negro church, causing the death of several American children.
True, the governor of Alabama has promised a reward for the apprehension of the culprits. But the real cause of these outrages was group defamation.
Then, I should like to read this paragraph:
We all know, already, that if a man should enter a crowded theatre and shout "fire" he soon will find out that he has violated a criminal statute. Clearly, his freedom of speech is not absolute.
If freedom of speech is not absolute, should freedom to defame large groups of fellow citizens remain absolute? We think not.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that the subject matter of this bill would be referred perhaps to the external affairs committee because of the commitment to the United Nations, so that this bill could be studied and the subject matter debated. Perhaps something could be evolved in this way that will protect ethnic groups. Every group in Canada is an ethnic group, even the founding races are ethnic groups. In a country such as Canada which is composed of so many different ethnic groups, surely a group libel law goes to the very essence of the unity of the country and protection against the destruction of democracy as we have seen it destroyed in Europe.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this house, and in fact all people, will share in the concern and apprehension of the hon. member with regard to the evil which he seeks to cure by this bill which he brings forward. The horrors which from time to time, the civilized world has had presented to it

through the medium of war trials and other means is undoubtedly a cause of great apprehension. In so far as the objective of the hon. member is concerned, I have no hesitation at all in saying that I am in fullest sympathy with him.
The thing is, however, do we by the means that he suggests actually cure this evil? Are there cures already in existence which could be applied? It is my philosophy, Mr. Speaker, that there is a tendency for governments to legislate in haste and amend at leisure. Legislating in haste is a sin of which this government could not be successfully accused, and I must put this as a condition to my remarks.

speechtext: That would be defamatory.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF PENALTIES UNDER UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION
speechtext:
Nevertheless, let us look at the law as it now exists. The hon. member will agree that a matter of such great importance as this, involving as it does the creation of a new offence punishable as capital murder, is one of great importance. This is especially true, having in mind the distinction which this parliament made between capital murder and non-capital murder. At the time this particular amendment to the Criminal Code was considered, these differences were most carefully weighed. At that time we considered most carefully the line of distribution as to what should be and could be included in capital murder and what should be kept on the other side of the boundary and found as non-capital murder.
This is important because, in effect, the first paragraph of the hon. member's bill would be doing violence to the changes in the Criminal Code represented by these amendments which this house and the other place considered most carefully. I would think that the gravest amount of care should be exercised before this is done. Apart from that, I want to make a submission with particular regard to the last two sections, numbered 3 and 4, of the proposed bill. I am not going to read those sections, but I am going to read three or four sections of the Criminal Code and I say that within the four corners of one or the other of those sections can be found a remedy which will meet the evil at which the hon. member is aiming. Before any bill such as this is enacted, I should like to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice that a particular act which the hon. member seeks to stress by this bill cannot be combated by making adequate use of the existing provisions of the Criminal Code.

Can the Minister of Justice stand before us and say that these provisions which the hon. member seeks to make part of the statute law of this country are absolutely essential to deal with the problem he has presented, because what we have now in the Criminal Code will not meet the situation? This, I think, is a condition precedent to this house actually dealing with this bill in the sense of enacting it. I do not know whether or not the hon. member has had these discussions. I do not know what the position of the Minister of Justice is, but this I think is something which could be considered.
I should like the hon. member when he closes the debate to recite any cases where informations have been laid and the cases have been proceeded with to the stage where a judicial decision has been made by a supreme court, district court, county court or appellate court on the type of act which he envisages in connection with this legislation. I think this is important, because when we enact legislation we do so for the reason there is nothing on the statute books to provide what we require.
I know there has been a lot of discussion in the newspapers and I think it is good there has been. I think it is a good thing that the hon. member has brought this bill forward so that it may be used as a catalyst to obtain some clarification of the ambiguity and obscurity which have surrounded this particular situation.
However, having said that I should like to refer very briefly to the third and fourth clauses of the bill, particularly the third clause. I am going to recite several sections of the Criminal Code because I wish to submit that under the circumstances of an offence being committed one cannot discount the possibility that it might be met by these sections of the Criminal Code. One of them is section 153, which might be termed a corollary because it does not go to the root of the matter. It reads as follows:
Everyone commits an offence who makes use of the mails for the purpose of transmitting or delivering anything that Is obscene, indecent, immoral or scurrilous-
It is the word "scurrilous" that I have in mind.
-but this section does not apply to a person who makes use of the mails for the purpose of transmitting or delivering-
And so on. This is an ancillary means of carrying into effect what the hon. gentleman aims to prevent, and I think this is one sec-
Genocide
tion which might be used under the circumstances. Section 165 reads as follows:
Everyone who commits a common nuisance and thereby... (a) endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public-
I will concede this is a little remote but I can conceive of situations where this particular section could be used and convictions could be secured under certain circumstances such as the hon. member has in mind. Section 166 reads as follows:
Everyone who wilfully publishes a statement, tale or news that he knows is false and that causes or is likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest-
"Public interest" is not defined, but I can conceive of a number of circumstances where a reasonable and apt interpretation of the words "public interest" would cover some of the situations which the hon. member has in mind. I also wish to refer to section 248 which deals with defamatory libel and reads as follows:
A defamatory libel is matter published, without lawful justification or excuse, that is likely to injure the reputation or any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule-
The hon. member quite properly pointed his finger at the word "person" and said that, the word "person" having been used in the Criminal Code, this automatically excludes actions which are directed against a class. At first blush I think that is a very sound argument, but I would refer the hon. member, who is from the province of Quebec, to a Quebec case. I do not have the case itself here, but it is referred to in The Canadian Abridgement, volume 13, and in column 436 I read these words:
...a charge of publishing a defamatory libel against the Roman Catholic clergy of a particular diocese does not disclose an offence. Section 317-
Which is now section 248.
-specifically refers to a ''person" and the definition of "person" in section 2 (13) is not sufficiently wide to include an unincorporated group-
The case goes on to use these words:
Although an indictment will lie at common law for libelling a class generally-
An indictment will lie at common law, and the common law is in effect in this country to the extent to which it has not been abrogated, altered or changed by our statute law.
-the indictment in such case must allege (and the crown must prove) that the tendency of the libel was to excite hatred against all members of the class and to provoke a breach of the peace.

Genocide
I would submit that those words meet squarely the problem which the bill aims to deal with. Finally, there is one more case I should like to refer members of the house to, a decision of that great old jurist, the late chief justice Harvey of the province of Alberta. In this case, which appears in column 140 of the same volume of The Canadian Abridgement, I find these words of the chief justice:
In Russell on Crimes It is stated that:
I am not going to take the time and trouble to read the definitions of sedition, seditious libel and so on because they have already been the subject of discussion in the house and the hon. member will know the precise wording.
-"Sedition consists In acts, words or writings intended or calculated under the circumstances of the time to disturb the tranquillity of the state by creating ill will, discontent, disafection, hatred or contempt towards the person of the kin, or toward the constitution or parliament"-
I think the words "or parliament" are words which some members of the public might well take note of at the present time.
-"or the government, or the established institutions of the country, or by exciting ill will between different classes of the king's subjects-
It is my submission that where there is a vacuum the common law applies. Wherever we have passed statutory enactments and occupied a vacuum, then the common law does not apply.
